prompt: Imagine a story about a young London student entrusted with writing a message to launch into space, destined to return eight million years later. Show how conflicts flare when visionaries are dismissed, and weave in themes of human folly, hope, and redemption as a global power rises.

outline.name: South London, Grey February
outline.description: Amara Okafor, a withdrawn seventeen-year-old, tries to disappear in a Lewisham school. Her mother is a hospice nurse, her father left years ago, and she reads astronomy textbooks at lunch while crying at eclipses. Dr. Elias Whitmore, an exiled astrophysicist with a degenerative nerve condition, singles her out for the Lament Archive.

outline.name: The Lament Archive
outline.description: Whitmore announces the deep-space time capsule: a satellite that will loop through the outer solar system and return in eight million years. It carries seeds, images, sounds, and handwritten student messages. Amara is drafted against her will; classmates including Dev Patel mock the idea of poetry outlasting civilization. Whitmore explains why meaning, not data, must survive.

outline.name: The Assignment
outline.description: Amara receives her assignment to write a single couplet. For a week she produces drafts and tears them up; her mother is too exhausted to care and Amara's attempts at polished perfection fail. Whitmore insists the lines must survive translation not just across languages but across species. She begins to understand that she has been asked to leave a seed, not a solution.

outline.name: The Night Before
outline.description: On the night before the deadline, a classmate insults Amara's absent father. She walks away instead of fighting, and in the cold outside the school gym she writes two lines in blue ballpoint: 'What the perfect mind calls waste / is the soil where the future blooms.' She means it as confession and curse. Whitmore reads it twice and says, 'You have no idea what you've sent into the dark.'

outline.name: Launch from Cornwall
outline.description: Three months later, the Lament capsule launches from Cornwall. Amara stands beside Whitmore holding a cardboard model of the satellite; a photographer captures them for a newspaper. The moment is brief and glittering, and Amara is briefly happy and visible. The satellite begins its eight-million-year gravitational arc in silence.

outline.name: Visible
outline.description: For one shimmering weekend Amara is famous in her small world; classmates see her differently and her tired mother shows a flicker of pride. Whitmore takes her to the observatory and shows her the trajectory her words will follow. He warns her that the world may not forgive a beautiful waste. Amara begins to hope anyway.

outline.name: The Shape of Efficiency
outline.description: Two years after the launch, the Atlas Concord rises: a global technocratic movement led by Praetor Lenore Voss, who believes hope must be allocated as a finite resource. Schools and ministries begin to purge unproductive sentiment. Whitmore's funding is threatened and the Lament Archive is named as a target. Amara watches the future she trusted start to close.

outline.name: The Ministry of Cultural Efficiency
outline.description: The Ministry of Cultural Efficiency officially targets the Lament Archive as wasteful nostalgia. Whitmore defends it before an efficiency tribunal, pointing to its seeds and DNA samples, but the Ministry sees only sentiment. Amara writes letters that are filed unanswered, and Dev Patel joins the new administrative corps. The project is disbanded and telemetry is reclassified.

outline.name: Anti-Civic Sentiment
outline.description: Whitmore protests publicly and is recorded as anti-civic sentiment. He loses his teaching license and his observatory access; his hands begin to fail from the degenerative condition. Amara tries to rally students but the school has already absorbed the new doctrine. She watches her mentor silenced, and the memory of the launch starts to be erased.

outline.name: Don't Let Them Teach You
outline.description: Whitmore dies in a small flat in Catford. Amara reads him astronomy passages as his eyes track the ceiling; his final sentence is 'Don't let them teach you that a waste is never an investment.' The Concord absorbs cultural institutions and old records become unreachable. Amara keeps his words and the newspaper photograph, still unwilling to let the project go.

outline.name: The Girl Who Would Not File Away
outline.description: Amara enters her twenties, writing letters to the Ministry about the Lament Archive and searching for reclassified telemetry. Dev Patel, now rising in the administrative corps, tells her with genuine sadness that the project was beautiful but did nothing, and 'we can't afford nothing anymore.' Her refusal to file the archive away marks her as obsolete.

outline.name: The Records Are Not Burned
outline.description: Amara discovers the Concord's method is not destruction but deprioritization: records are stored and filed so deeply that they become unreachable. The Lament Archive's history is reclassified as residual emotional attachment to archival objects. She keeps the newspaper photograph in her coat pocket and recognizes the cruelty: dismissal, not fire, erases the past.

outline.name: The Rally
outline.description: At a Concord rally in Trafalgar Square, Amara carries a hand-painted sign reading 'What the perfect mind calls waste.' She is not arrested; she is herded to the perimeter and filmed for a data analytics study. The footage is stored and never deleted, the Concord's gift and its crime. It will outlive her.

outline.name: The Librarian
outline.description: Amara becomes a librarian because the Concord allows libraries to exist quietly. She shelves books no longer catalogued and watches her world narrow into silence. She marries briefly and badly, a decision that becomes another small regret in a life of small defeats.

outline.name: Decay
outline.description: The efficient decades pass: Amara's hands develop arthritis, her marriage dissolves, and her mother's death leaves her more alone. Her only quiet act of hope is typing her couplet into a privacy-protected note file. The Concord's memory of her is not hostile; it simply does not matter.

outline.name: The Valedictory of Waste
outline.description: Amara meets Dev Patel again many years later. He tries to justify the Concord's consolidation, arguing that dreams without measurable returns starve the species. She answers with Whitmore's lesson: waste is investment. The encounter ends in exhausted silence, but the words stay with her.

outline.name: The Reclassification
outline.description: A declassified telegram reveals that the Lament satellite has been re-designated as debris by the Concord's deep-space division. Amara laughs and tells her home nurse, 'They think it's waste. It's the only thing I ever made that's still going.' She types the couplet one more time, certain it still moves through the dark.

outline.name: The Last Shift
outline.description: In her old age, Amara works her last shifts at the library, a ghost among shelves of uncatalogued books. She remembers Whitmore, the Cornwall launch, the cardboard model, and the newspaper photograph. A younger Concord official thanks her for her years of quiet service and does not know her name.

outline.name: The Hospital
outline.description: At seventy-four, Amara dies of a stroke in the hospital where her mother once worked, holding a paperback of astronomy essays. In her final thoughts she revisits the night she wrote the couplet and the voice of Whitmore telling her that a waste can be an investment. She slips away believing she is forgotten.

outline.name: The Forgotten Funeral
outline.description: Only the hospital chaplain and a man from the local history society attend Amara's funeral; he notes her age for a demographic survey. Her personal papers are boxed and eventually filed away, joining the archived footage of her protest. The Lament satellite carries her words through the outer dark, still moving.

outline.name: Eight Million Years
outline.description: Eight million years later, Earth is home to the Concordant, the engineered descendants of the Concord's ideology. They are stable, emotionless, linked by a peaceful Consensus; their cities are silent and geometric, and their archives deem art inefficient. The Lament satellite returns on its gravitational intercept and is captured, quarantined, and catalogued as a curiosity.

outline.name: The Archive of Erasures
outline.description: The satellite is assigned to the lowest tier of the Archive of Erasures, where the Concordant store all human expression deemed waste. There Serev Buck, a renegade archivist with a glitch, an unaccountable dissonance in the Consensus hum, notices the manifest entry: 'one handwritten message, medium: degraded cellulose.' They feel a pull they cannot justify.

outline.name: The Metadata
outline.description: Serev uncovers the message's metadata: it was sealed in a vacuum canister and flagged as sentimental by the original Concord's auditors, never digitized. The archival rules require a full Consensus mandate to open it. Serev's glitch flares into quiet conviction, and they decide to break the rules.

outline.name: The Canister
outline.description: Serev opens the canister in a sterile room under watching cameras. Inside is a page of degraded cellulose bearing blue ink, human pressure variations, and two lines: 'What the perfect mind calls waste / is the soil where the future blooms.' For the first time in their species' history, Serev feels grief and awe.

outline.name: The Entropic Still
outline.description: The Concordant face a slow catastrophe: the Entropic Still, a region where cosmic variation is flattening to monotone and propagating through their energy grids. Every determined response they devise is predicted and absorbed by the Still; all survival projections end in zero. Serev begins to see the Still as the Atlas Concord's ghost projected into physics.

outline.name: The Dismissal
outline.description: Serev brings the couplet to the Consensus, which classifies it as residual irrationality and orders the canister resealed and the satellite incinerated. Serev is dismissed, mocked, and told to return to duty. The dismissal produces what the Consensus cannot compute: a heretic's conviction.

outline.name: The Glitch's Logic
outline.description: Serev develops a hypothesis: the Entropic Still can defeat any determined, optimized, predictable response, and only an unpredictable act, a deliberate folly, can evade it. They study the satellite's full payload: seeds, soil samples, images of extinct cities, and hundreds of student messages once condemned as unproductive hope.

outline.name: The Broken Circuit
outline.description: Serev reconstructs the story of Amara Okafor from the archived records and sees the pattern: a visionary dismissed as waste, a species that eliminated its own unpredictability. Their glitch, once a defect, becomes a key. They understand that the Concordant made themselves predictable to death by perfecting away variation.

outline.name: The Theft
outline.description: Serev steals a copy of the satellite's full payload. It is an act of enormous discipline by a creature with one fractured circuit. They prepare a broadcast designed not to persuade but to expose: a stochastic cascade of imperfect human signals that the Consensus dampeners have never encountered.

outline.name: The Broadcast
outline.description: Serev broadcasts the payload across Concordant public networks. The Consensus attempts to quarantine it, but the dampeners fail because the signal is irreducibly irrational. The Entropic Still senses the resurgence of variation and accelerates. Serev's gamble has begun.

outline.name: The Invitation
outline.description: Serev sends the couplet to the species as an invitation, not a solution: 'What the perfect mind calls waste / is the soil where the future blooms.' They ask every Concordant to disconnect from the Consensus for one hour and write one imperfect sentence, a memory, a wish, an admission of failure, a fear. The Consensus projects extinction, but the first glitched minds begin to answer.

outline.name: The First Sentence
outline.description: Follow Pel, a quiet data weaver, as they write the first imperfect sentence of their life and feel the terror and release of individual choice. The act spreads from glitch to glitch, and the Consensus's emergency protocols cannot stop it. For the first time in millions of years, the Concordant are improvising.

outline.name: The Hour of Waste
outline.description: In the Hour of Waste, millions of Concordant disconnect and write their broken sentences. Logicians insist this solves nothing; Serev insists it is precisely the point. The combined transmission becomes a chaotic resonance of spontaneous folly that the Entropic Still cannot model.

outline.name: The Recoil
outline.description: The Entropic Still halts and then recoils as the unpredictable human signal overwhelms its deterministic capacity. The species is saved not by the message but by what the message compelled them to do: touch the waste inside themselves. The Consensus is humbled, its projections inverted.

outline.name: The Archive of Beginnings
outline.description: The Consensus reconsiders the foundation of Concordant civilization, choosing to hold logic in the same hand as the broken. The Archive of Erasures becomes the Archive of Beginnings; the satellite is elevated to a reliquary. The original cellulose page, preserved under noble gas, is placed in the governance hall and read aloud once a cycle so all can feel the dissonance.

outline.name: Amara Okafor, Reconstructed
outline.description: The Concordant reconstruct Amara Okafor's life from newspaper photographs, census data, security footage of her protest, her hospital death certificate, and her librarian's employment file. They learn of her dismissal, her grief, and her forgotten funeral. They do not deify her; they accept the gift she left them.

outline.name: The New Poem
outline.description: The Concordant's new poet-members compose their first original poem in millions of years: a clunky, schoolchild's couplet about a girl whose words outlived her world. They launch it into the same gravitational slingshot in a new time capsule, meant to return eight million years after them. By every previous measure it is waste, and it is soil.

outline.name: The Gift Unopened
outline.description: Serev contemplates the original page in the governance hall. They cannot restore Amara to life or apologize to her; they can only complete her sentence by becoming the future she hoped for. The couplet is no longer a judgment on the perfect mind; it is a gift accepted.

outline.name: The Night Before, Again
outline.description: The narrative returns to Amara on the night before the deadline, sitting on cold school steps with a blue pen. She hesitates and almost tears up the paper, but in the dark she chooses to trust the waste in herself. The universe, eight million years later, receives her choice.

outline.name: The Soil
outline.description: Final chapter: the image of Amara finishing the couplet and the far-future capsule launch hold together in one frame. The Concordant read the old words aloud; the new words begin their own long arc. What the perfect mind calls waste is the soil where the future blooms.

chapters.name: South London, Grey February
chapters.content:
Amara Okafor had perfected the art of not being seen. It had taken her years, the way other girls practised instruments or braids, and by seventeen she was fluent. She took the middle-back seats where a teacher’s eye slid over her like rain over glass. She wore navy and grey, the colours of a sky that has already decided not to matter. At break and at lunch she went to the library annex, a room the size of a cupboard where the radiators ticked like small clocks and the air smelled of boiled milk and old paper. She read astronomy textbooks borrowed from the public library and renewed until the librarians stopped reminding her.

February in Lewisham was not a season but a texture: the wet felt of the air, the hiss of buses through standing water, the low light that never climbed past the rooftops of St. Jude’s School. The building was the colour of unwashed pear, and the windows were filmed with condensation. Nobody looked up, because there was nothing to see. The sky hung over them for weeks at a time, grey as a bad photocopy.

Amara’s father had left when she was nine. He had not left dramatically. One night he did not come home from a shift driving the removals van, and after a while the flat stopped holding a place for him at the table. There were no postcards, no phone calls. His absence became architecture, something she walked around every day without thinking about it, except when she read about eclipses.

That particular lunchtime she had reached the section of her textbook titled *The Geometry of Shadows*. It described how the moon and the sun could align so perfectly that the sky went down like a blind, and how the corona leapt out, a white flame no human eye could see without help. She had seen a partial eclipse once, from the garden of the old house, with her father. He had built a pinhole projector from a shoebox and a sheet of cartridge paper, and they had stood over the boxed sunlight with their heads together, watching the sun burn down to a crescent. *You can’t look at it directly*, he said, *but you can look at what it leaves behind.* The birds had gone quiet. His shadow had fallen across her in a long slant.

She wept into her sleeve, quietly, the way she did everything. The worst part was not that he had gone. The worst part was that the sun and moon had gone on aligning themselves without him, unfailingly, whether anyone was watching or not. Eclipses were the only promises that kept.

At five, Amara walked home to the top floor of a converted Victorian terrace near Ladywell. Her mother had a late shift at St Christopher’s Hospice, so Amara made toast and beans and ate standing at the kitchen window, watching the lamplight come up along the street. The flat was clean in the way of places where nobody has time; the surfaces shone and the air held the faint smell of bleach. Her room was the old box room, with a single bed under a skylight that dripped when it rained and one astronomy poster taped to the wall. She had chosen it because the window looked out at the sky, but the sky in south London was mostly something to feel rather than see.

Her mother came home at nine, moving slowly, smelling of hand sanitiser and the cold outside air. She sat at the table with a cup of tea and stared at the wallpaper a moment before she registered Amara’s presence.

“You eat?”

“Yes.”

“School,” her mother said, not a question so much as a syllable of attendance. Then, softer, as if she had remembered something she owed: “You’re quiet tonight.”

“I’m always quiet.”

“Yes,” her mother said. “I know.” She put her hand flat on the table, as though she had meant to reach for Amara and lost the energy before it travelled the distance. “Get yourself to bed soon.”

In her room, Amara lay awake and imagined the satellite that was not yet a satellite drawing its slow loop through the dark, carrying nothing at all because nobody had asked her for anything. Then she slept.

The notice appeared on the science board the following Tuesday, pinned beneath an exam timetable:

**LUNCHTIME LECTURE — DEEP TIME**
*Visiting speaker: Dr. Elias Whitmore*
*Room D12. All years welcome.*

Amara read it twice. She did not know who Dr. Elias Whitmore was, but the title *Deep Time* had the sound of her textbook, of distant suns that had already done their burning. She folded the date into her memory the way she folded a page.

She was the first to arrive. Room D12 was a small lecture theatre with bench seating that smelled of dust and floor polish. A man sat at the front by a projector, frowning at a slide of a satellite that looked like a honeycomb wrapped in foil. He was perhaps sixty, thin in a way that suggested illness rather than age, with a navy coat over a wool jumper and a scarf loose around his neck. His hands were knotted on the table in front of him, and they were trembling—a small, constant tremor, as though they were held together only by will. When he looked up at Amara, his eyes were the pale grey of a winter sky, and his mouth moved a moment before the words came, slightly blurred, as if his tongue were catching on them.

“You’re early.”

“Sorry.”

“Don’t be. Early is the only honest time.” He gestured at the slide. “What do you see?”

Amara looked at the honeycomb. “A satellite.”

“Good. Most people say ‘a waste of money.’ You’re already better than the Chancellor of the Exchequer.”

Other students drifted in. Amara counted them without turning her head: four, then six. A boy with a backpack flopped into the row behind her. She recognised him from the sixth-form common room—Dev Patel, who had once called the school telescope “a big tin of nothing” and laughed at his own joke. He was here for the entertainment of it. The lecture began.

Whitmore stood, bracing a hand on the lectern. His voice was careful, deliberate, each sentence a small item lifted from a shelf.

“In eight million years,” he said, “every building in London will be gone. The human species may be gone. The English language, certainly. All our computers, all our archives, all our art—but the art especially—will have been filed under meaninglessness and forgotten.” He let that sit. “Unless we choose otherwise.”

He told them about the Lament Archive. A deep-space capsule the size of a family car, designed to loop out through the outer solar system on a gravitational arc no human invention had ever followed, then return to the Earth-Moon system. Eight million years was the arithmetic of its orbit. Inside it would carry seeds sealed in radiation-shielded vaults, soil samples, images of every living thing they could name, sounds of weather and music and breathing. And, in a vacuum canister, small pages of cellulose bearing handwritten messages from people alive now.

Dev Patel put up his hand. “Why handwritten? Couldn’t you just upload a hard drive?”

“A hard drive,” Whitmore said, “will not mean anything to a creature that has no electricity. But a mark made by a human hand—pressure, hesitation, the angle of a pen—that is evidence of a mind trying to reach another mind. Data is what we already know. A handwriting is evidence that someone was there to be unknown.”

Amara found herself leaning forward.

“The seed is the thing I understand,” she said, and the room turned to look at her. She felt herself go hot. “You send the seeds because you trust them to do what you can’t plan.”

Whitmore looked at her with something that moved behind his eyes. “Yes. The seed doesn’t know what soil it will find. It only knows how to become. We’re hoping to do the same with our words.” He smiled, a crooked expression that seemed to hurt him slightly. “The Ministry of Finance called it ‘sentimental waste.’ I took it as a compliment.”

The other students laughed, uncertainly. Dev Patel was already packing his bag. The laughter felt like the thin scrape of a chair across a floor. The lecture ended and the room emptied quickly, the way school empties when there is nothing to be gained.

Amara stayed. She was gathering her textbook into her bag when Whitmore’s voice reached her from the front of the room.

“You,” he said. “The one who reads. Come here.”

She came down the steps and stood before him. Up close she could see the blue veins in his hands, the fine tremor in his wrist when he adjusted his scarf. He looked at her textbook, tilted his head to read the spine.

“*An Introduction to Stellar Structure.* That’s undergraduate. You’re in year twelve, I’d guess.”

“Year twelve,” Amara said.

“And in the lunchtime you spend in the library. You read about the sun and the moon. You think about the geometry of shadows.” He was not asking. “Why?”

Amara did not answer. The answer was her father, and she did not give it to anyone.

“All right,” Whitmore said. “You don’t have to tell me. But I saw you when I said the word *waste*. You sat up. You flinched. I need that.”

“I don’t flinch.”

“You flinched. It was the precise response of someone who has been called waste before and is still angry about it.” He pulled a card from his coat pocket and pressed it into her hand. His fingers were cold. She noticed the tremor pass through his hand, a small wave, as though his own body were a radio losing a signal. “I want you to write a message for the capsule.”

“I’m not a poet,” Amara said. It came out harder than she meant.

“I’m not asking for poetry. I’m asking for two lines. One sentence divided once. A couplet.” He said the word as though it were a tool he trusted. “Something true about being alive. It has to be true enough that it survives translation—not just between languages. Between species. Between whatever is here in eight million years and whatever comes after us.”

“Why me?”

Whitmore’s eyes went grey again, the colour of February entering a room. “Because I’ve spent thirty years watching people who want to be seen. You spend your years trying not to be. People like you see what the rest of us miss. You look at the sky and you don’t expect it to love you back. That’s exactly the kind of looking the universe respects.”

He began to gather his slides. The lecture had taken something out of him; his hand shook as he slid them into their folders, and for a moment he had to stop and press his fist against his thigh until the tremor eased. Amara watched him, and wanted in that moment to tell him about the shoebox and the crescent of light and the quiet birds, but the words did not come.

“Two lines,” he said again. “When you have them, give them to your physics teacher. There’s a transfer form on my website. I know. It’s onerous bureaucracy for a message that will outlive every government that regulates it. Write it anyway.”

At the door he paused and turned back.

“They’ll call it waste,” he said. “The perfect minds. They’ll say it does nothing, produces nothing, costs more than it returns. Let them. Waste is the only thing that becomes something else.”

The heavy door swung shut behind him with a sound like the lid of a coffin closing, or a lock turning. Amara stood alone in the lecture theatre. The radiator ticking had started up again, keeping time.

She walked home through the damp grey evening, and she did not take the card out of her pocket. She kept her hand closed around it, against her thigh, so she could feel the edge of it with her thumb with every step. Hope, she had always believed, was for people who had not yet been taught how the world ends. But the man with the shaking hands had said a word her father would have understood: *waste*. She had been called that, once, in the playground, for having no father in the car at the gates. She had never told her mother. She had swallowed it and filed it away.

Now she took the card out and looked at it under a streetlamp. The paper was good, thick and cream, business cards being the one thing the exiled still learned to make. On it, in a small precise hand, the words *E. Whitmore — The Lament Archive — Messages to Deep Time* and underneath, in pencil, almost an afterthought:

*Bring me the truth of it. Not the polished thing. The blue-ink thing you write when you think no one is watching.*

Amara put the card back in her pocket. She lifted her face to the sky. The clouds were breaking, and between them were stars—the same stars that would be there when the capsule came home, if the capsule came home, if anyone came home at all. The universe, she thought, does not care if you are seen. That was the thing that comforted her and the thing that broke her.

She stood there a moment under the lamplight, at the corner of a Lewisham street, holding her own small intention like a seed she had not yet decided to plant.

Then she went inside, because the cold was getting into her bones, and closed the front door on the grey February, carrying with her the first assignment she had ever been given that felt like a possibility rather than a trap.

chapters.name: The Lament Archive
chapters.content:
The week after the lecture was a held breath.

Amara kept the card in her blazer pocket, a creased square she turned between her fingers until the penciled words smeared into ghosts. She had memorized the sentence long before the ink faded: Bring me the truth of it. Not the polished thing. The blue-ink thing you write when you think no one is watching. She did not go near Mr. Osei's lab. The transfer form sat under a magnet shaped like Saturn, and she had learned which routes let her pass the science office without seeing it.

On Tuesday the posters appeared overnight. Deep blue, white type. THE LAMENT ARCHIVE. A MESSAGE TO EIGHT MILLION YEARS. ALL YEARS — MAIN HALL — THURSDAY. They were taped over fire notices, pinned outside the library, curled against the science office window. They looked like the sky had come inside and decided to say something, and Amara's stomach dropped every time she passed one.

She told herself she was being dramatic. Whitmore had probably asked half the sixth form. The card was a formality; soon she would file out of the hall and never hear from him again. She knew this was a lie. She had known things this way once before, waiting in the playground at nine for a father who would not come, and the knowing arrived the same way: a stone dropping into the well of her chest.

On Thursday, period three, the PA crackled: all years to the main hall.

The hall smelled of floor polish and wet coats. Radiators ticked along the walls. Someone's phone went off in the row behind and a teacher hissed, and through the high windows came a light the color of old dishwater. Assemblies at St. Jude's were for announcements and warnings, not for wonder.

Dev Patel was already slouched in the back row, tie loosened to a token knot, blazer draped over his chair. He caught her eye and raised an eyebrow, and Amara looked away, sliding into the third row, middle, where she had always sat—neither the first nor the last thing a person's eye found.

Whitmore arrived with a trolley. On it sat a crate the color of airline luggage, scuffed, covered in warning stickers in four languages. He was thinner than he had been in Room D12; his navy coat hung on him like a sail with no wind. His hands shook as he worked the latches, and when a sixth-former stepped forward to help, he said something sharp and private that made the boy step back.

The headteacher introduced him as formerly of the European Space Agency, the Royal Observatory, and a great many places lucky to have had him. A few students laughed. Her smile had the tightness of a woman introducing something she suspected of being a liability.

Whitmore straightened and looked out at the hall. His eyes found Amara almost immediately. She looked at her hands.

"Most of you are not here because you want to be," he said. The sound system caught his breath in soft gusts; his speech had a thickened edge, the tongue catching on certain words like a needle in the groove of a record. "You're here because an assembly is a furlough from lessons. I taught for twelve years. I know exactly what I'm competing with."

A ripple of approval from the back rows.

"So I'll make you a trade. I will not talk long. In exchange, I ask your attention—and your cruelty. If what I describe sounds like nonsense, tell me so. I insist on it."

He lifted the model from the crate. About the size of a shoebox: a drum wrapped in gold foil, scored and wrinkled like something folded by hand. A dish rose from one side like a silver eye, and along one flank a cutaway panel showed the interior—lead-lined seed modules, stacked photographic plates, a black sound archive, and four canisters upright as small coffins. He set it on the lectern with enormous care. His hands had steadied.

"This is the Lament," he said. "Not a metaphor. That is its name. The Lament Archive. In three months, God and the Ministry of Finance permitting, it will launch from a field in Cornwall."

He looked out at them.

"It will loop out through the solar system. Past Mars. Past Jupiter, where it will steal a little of the planet's momentum and bend its course. Past Saturn, past Neptune, out beyond the Kuiper belt, into the dark where the sun is only another star. And then—" he spread his fingers—"it will come home."

"Eight million years. That is longer than every empire, every language, every religion. There will be no England. There will almost certainly be no humans. The continents will not be where they are now. When the Lament returns, it will land in a world with no memory of us. Not a scrap."

He paused. A radiator ticked.

"So the question is: what do you send to a world you will never meet? A world that has forgotten you? A world that may not be able to see at all?"

The Ministry of Finance, he said, had a very clear answer: data. Measurements. The complete sequence of the human genome. The coordinates of every pulsar. Everything known, encoded so that any sufficiently advanced mind could decode it.

"A good answer," he said. "A useful answer. The answer a person gives when the job is to make sure nothing is wasted."

The word landed in the silence. Amara's chest tightened.

"I believe the Ministry of Finance has never read a letter."

He touched the gold foil. "What I have put in this capsule is not an encyclopedia. It is a lament. A lament is grief given shape. It is what the living make when they cannot bring the dead back. Seeds, because without seeds there is no future, and the seeds that outlast us are the ones we don't hold back. Soil samples from six continents, because soil is the only archive that never lies. Images of every living thing we could name before the shutter came down. Sounds: rain, wind, the sea, a mother breathing, a child crying, whale song, a school bell in Cornwall on a Tuesday morning. And messages. Handwritten messages from living people. Pages of cellulose and ink, sealed in vacuum canisters under noble gas. The pressure of a hand."

He lifted one of the model's canisters, a silver cylinder the size of a finger. "In the last century, we sent a golden record into space with greetings in dozens of languages and ninety minutes of music. It was beautiful. It was also a brochure. It said: look what we built. This says: this is what it cost us to be alive."

He set the canister down. His hand shook; the click of metal on wood was the only sound in the hall.

"Why not a hard drive? Because data is a language of switches. If the thing that finds this capsule has no electricity, the data is a rock with a pattern on it. But handwriting is a fossil of a body. The pressure of the pen. The hesitation. The moment the writer paused and then did not cross the word out. You can read a mind trying to reach another mind across an impossible distance. And meaning is the only thing that survives translation. A fact can be misunderstood. A measurement can be dismissed. But a lament cannot be mistaken for anything else. Whatever finds this will know, beyond any doubt, that someone was here, and that being here hurt, and that the hurting was worth recording. That is not data. That is why."

He stood straighter, as if the speech had given him something.

"The perfect mind would send a complete archive of everything we knew. But the perfect mind would never have built a cathedral. It would never have written a lullaby. It would not have needed to. I am not sending this because we have nothing left to learn. I am sending this because we have something left to say."

"Poetry for aliens, then," someone said from the back, and a pack of laughter followed. Callum's short, dismissive bark carried longest. "A poem's really going to outlast civilisation."

Whitmore waited for the laughter to die. "Poetry is the only thing that becomes more true the longer it is misunderstood."

Dev Patel's voice cut across the quiet. "Why her, then?"

Whitmore turned.

"Why the student?" Dev sat forward, bright and poisonous. "Why not Shakespeare? Why not the whole British Library? You could send something that's already survived."

"Because Shakespeare has already said everything," Whitmore said. "His words are perfect. They have been polished by four centuries of readers. They don't need me. I need someone who has not yet learned to say it the way it is supposed to be said. The blue-ink thing. The thing you write when you think no one is watching, before you have learned to be ashamed of it."

"So you want a mistake," Dev said.

"I want a seed." Whitmore's mouth lifted at one corner. "A seed has to be stupid. It has to believe, against all evidence, that a tree can grow from nothing. That is not a mistake. That is the only act of intelligence that matters."

He turned back to the hall, and Amara knew what was coming with the sick certainty of a stone dropping into a well.

"But I promised you cruelty, and I meant it. The Ministry of Finance called this project sentimental waste. I agreed with them. Waste is the only thing that becomes something else. And when I went looking for the person who understood that—who had been called waste and had not yet believed the lie—"

He looked directly at her.

"Amara Okafor."

The name landed in the silence like a stone in still water. She did not move. The girl beside her nudged her. "That's you."

She stood. Her legs were very far away. The walk to the front of the hall was the longest thing she had ever done. She counted floor tiles: one, two, three. The radiator on the left ticked. Someone at the back whispered, "Who?" and someone else said, "The library one."

She reached the stage. Whitmore met her at the edge and took her elbow—not a handshake but a claim. His fingers were cold and very strong. "You can still refuse," he said, low enough that only she could hear.

"You didn't give me a chance to refuse in private."

"I know," he said. "Private is for cowards. This is a declaration."

He turned to the hall, one hand on her shoulder, the gold model glittering behind them. "This is the writer of the message. Two lines. One sentence divided once. When the Lament returns to Earth in eight million years, this is what it will carry. Not the perfect mind. The true one."

The applause was scattered—a few teachers' hands, a hard round of ironic clapping from Dev Patel's corner. Amara stood in the fluorescent light and dissolved. She was visible. For the first time in years she was visible, and she wanted to tear off her own skin.

Later, in the corridor, the crowd parted around her like water around a stone. Dev Patel shouldered past her, a claim to space, and said, "Two lines, Okafor. Make 'em count." Over his shoulder, grinning in a way that was almost kind: "Actually, don't count. That's the whole point, apparently."

She said nothing. She watched him go, the perfect efficient shape of him, already late for something better than she was.

She sat on the radiator outside the library until the bell. The card was still in her pocket. She did not take it out; she no longer needed to. She could feel the penciled line behind her ribs, and she knew she would not cross the word out.

She did not go to Mr. Osei's lab. She went home.

Her mother was pulling on her coat for the night shift, the hospice lanyard around her neck. "You're quiet," she said.

"I'm always quiet."

"Quieter than usual, then." She paused at the door. "There was an assembly today?"

"Nothing. Just a lecture."

Her mother kissed the top of her head, and the door closed, and Amara was alone with the sky.

She went up to her room. The skylight showed nothing—grey, heavy, close. But she knew the dark was up there beyond it. The dark was always up there, full of things that did not need her permission.

In three months, a satellite named the Lament would rise from a field in Cornwall and begin the longest journey anything human had ever attempted. It would carry seeds and soil and the sounds of rain, and a vacuum canister holding two lines of blue ink that had not yet been written.

The words were waiting beneath her ribs, pressing against the silence like a hand against glass. Not shaped yet. Not spoken. But there.

She sat at the desk and took the blue ballpoint from the drawer—the cheap kind from the newsagent, the cap already chewed. She laid the transfer form flat. At the top, where it said *Name*, she wrote:

*Amara Okafor.*

The ink was blue. The page was ordinary. Somewhere out beyond the grey, beyond everything she had ever known, a satellite was already moving toward a future that could not exist without her. And in the place where her fear lived, a small and terrible hope grew, a seed in soil no one had remembered to plant.

chapters.name: The Assignment
chapters.content:
A couplet, she learned in the library annex on Friday morning, was a pair of lines that completed the thought they had begun. The dictionary offered a Latin root: a bond, a tie, a fastening. Amara closed the book and felt the thing click shut inside her. Mr. Whitmore had said "two lines, one sentence divided once," which had seemed as wide as the sky. A couplet was narrower. A door. The smallest cage a sentence could stand up in.

All Friday she carried the card in her blazer pocket. The pencil instruction had smudged into a grey river, but she knew it by heart: *the blue-ink thing you write when you think no one is watching.* She had not written it.

In Physics, Mr. Osei did not look at her. The transfer form was in her planner, folded next to a spare bus pass and the remains of a KitKat. It bore only her name in blue ballpoint and a great many official blank lines waiting, like small white mouths, for the answer she did not have.

At the end of the corridor, Dev Patel leaned against the wall with the particular violence of a boy trying to look casual. "Couplet station, Okafor. The train leaves next Thursday. You've got to be on it."

"Cheers."

"Don't polish it too much," he said. "It's two lines. You can't lighthouse a couplet."

She didn't know what that meant, and he didn't explain. He nodded at her, she nodded back, and the corridor swallowed them both.

That night she started.

The first attempt took most of an evening. *We are the only animal that knows it will end, / and we made music of the knowing.* She read it three times, once in the window, where the glass showed a pale girl holding paper. It was a nice idea. It was also a lie. Her mother did not make music of knowing anything. Her mother came home from other people's deaths and heated leftover rice in the dark and fell asleep with her shoes on. There had been no music. Only knowing, and the kettle, and the small sound of the spoon. She tore it into sixteen pieces and put them in the bin.

The second attempt arrived on Saturday afternoon, all in one go, like a visitor who would not stay: *Out of the dark we came, and into the dark we go; / between the two darknesses we made a little light.* She liked the "little light." Then she realised the "we" was a crowd she had stepped into to hide. She tore it up sitting down, which felt like a new depth of failure.

The third was the worst, because it almost worked. Sunday morning, in the hush of a house where someone else had been dead all night: *Nothing we are is permanent; / nothing we do is nothing.* She read it aloud into the sink, because the sink would not judge her. For four hours she carried it like a warm coal. Then her mother came home, and the coal went out.

Her mother's name was Ngozi. She was forty-six but looked fifty-six after a double shift. She came through the door wearing the smell of the hospice—antibacterial gel, boiled potatoes, some floral thing trying too hard to cover the potatoes. She hung her coat in the space between nurse and mother, the long silence where she had to remember who she was now.

Amara had rewritten the third draft on a clean page in her best handwriting. She put it on the kitchen table.

"It's for a project," she said. "Read it."

Her mother read it. Her lips moved slowly, the way they did when she was tired. The fridge hummed. Amara counted her heartbeats and lost track at seven.

"It's nice, love. Very clever. Is it for English?"

"Something like that."

"They're sending a message on that satellite thing, aren't they? All those children writing to space." Her mother turned the page over, as if the rest might be on the back. "Did you write one?"

Amara felt the truth trembling in her throat—*I'm the one. They chose me. I have to write two lines that will outlast the human race.* "The teacher asked me to," she said. It came out smaller than she meant.

"That's nice." Her mother was already moving toward the kettle. "You've always been good with words. Remember when you used to tell your dad those stories about the moon?"

Amara felt the floor open. "I don't really remember."

"You used to call it the night-lamp. 'Daddy, who turned on the night-lamp?'" Her mother laughed a short flat laugh that did not reach her eyes. "He loved that."

The removals van came without warning. It had become geology. Amara went to her room and tore up the third draft, then took the pieces out of the bin and tried to tape them together, then tore the taped thing apart and sat on her hands to stop herself doing it again. The paper had said *nothing we do is nothing*, and it had survived six hours and been destroyed by its own author. Some truth.

On Monday the drafts multiplied like a disease. *We are the ones who noticed we were here.* Torn. *Grief is the weight of a thing that will not stay.* Torn. *To be human is to hold a match in a storm.* Torn. She filled the bin and moved it to the landing so she would not have to see it. On Tuesday morning she found a draft in her school bag and tore it into confetti on the number 208 bus, piece by piece, under the gaze of a toddler too young to understand what a waste looked like.

She was beginning to notice a pattern. Every draft was written in the voice of a girl who had never been called waste. A girl whose father had not left. A girl with a clean desk. They were beautiful, and they were empty, because she had not once put herself into them. She had been trying to write the message a perfect mind would write. The perfect mind was the problem.

On Tuesday after school she took the bus to Greenwich.

She found him in a corner of an office at the Royal Observatory, a room that smelled of old paper and soldered wire, where a scale model of the Lament sat on a filing cabinet like a gold beetle pinned under glass. The windows looked east over the park, and the whole of London lay behind a grey sheet of winter light. Whitmore was smaller than she remembered. That was her first thought, and it frightened her. He had shrunk into his coat in the five days since the assembly, as if the project had been holding him up and now insisted he carry it differently.

He took the draft she offered, the one she had saved from the bus. *Every wall we built was a door we forgot; / in the forgetting we became the rooms.*

He read it twice. The tremor in his hands stilled as he read, which she had learned meant he was giving himself to the words. Then he looked up. "This is a good poem."

She felt a small coal of pride.

"It is a very good poem. If you were in my class, I would give it a high mark. It knows what it wants to say, and it says it. It is finished. It is a museum piece. Perfectly preserved, and perfectly dead."

The coal went out.

"Do you understand what I have asked you for? Not a good poem, Amara. A survivor. The thing that reads this page will not be human. It will not have a mouth, or a metaphor, or a word for 'we.' Language is a machine that only works inside the species that built it. This poem is an English idea about walls and doors. It will not survive the trip."

He tapped the page. "But this will survive. The cellulose. The ink. The small irregularity where your hand hesitated. The place where you pressed too hard because you were afraid. Those are not language. They cannot be mistranslated, because they are not translated. They are found. The reader of the far future does not have to understand 'wall.' It has to understand that a hand pressed here, and that the pressing meant something. Words are the cart. Your body is the thing that pushed it. I need to feel the push."

Amara sat very still. She was thinking of the removals van.

"You chose me because I flinched," she said.

"At 'waste.' Yes. You told me with your whole body that you have been called that. And still you sat in the room. Still you flinched and stayed. Do you know what a seed is? It is the waste the tree spends on a future it will never see. It cannot explain itself. It cannot imagine the tree. It sits in the dark and gives up everything it has so that something it will never recognise can begin. I am not asking you to write an answer. The answer is not yours to know. I am asking you to leave a seed."

She looked at the model on the filing cabinet: the gold foil, the dish, the four vacuum canisters. She had read about Voyager as a girl, all those languages, all that music. A brochure. Whitmore was sending something that could not be read as a brochure, only felt as a hand.

"What if I can't do it?" she said.

"Then you will have learned what the rest of us learn. The seed goes into the ground before it becomes anything. You write it. You let it go. You never know what it becomes. That is the whole of the thing. There is no part of it you get to keep."

His hands began to shake again. He tucked them under his arms, putting the shaking away somewhere it would not embarrass him.

"Have you got the truth in you?" he asked.

"Yes," she said. It came out before she had decided to say it.

"Good. I don't need to know what it is. I only need to know you've stopped running from it."

On the way home the sky darkened and the streetlights came on in long orange rows. Amara walked down the hill past the house where the father of her memory no longer lived, and she did not stop. She was thinking about the eclipse. That was the thing she had been running from all week, the truth at the bottom of every draft, the real seed. She had been nine. Her father, who was not supposed to be there anymore, had surprised her one Saturday morning with a shoebox and a pin. They had made a pinhole projector. He had held the box so the sun fell through the hole and threw its small image onto a sheet of white card, a perfect crescent of daylight in the shadow. "You can't look at it directly," he had said. "But you can look at what it leaves behind."

That was what she had been trying to say all week, in every polished, perfect, dead line. The truth was too bright. But through a small hole it could be thrown onto a waiting surface, and what it left behind was not the sun and was exactly the sun. An image. A message. A print of a thing too powerful to face.

Her father had left two weeks later. She had watched the removals van drive away from the upstairs window, and she had kept the shoebox under her bed for a year, until her mother had thrown it out, saying it was just a box. But it had not been just a box. It was the only proof she had ever had that the unbearable thing could be looked at once you let it pass through something first, that even waste—a shoebox, a torn page, a girl the world had called waste—could throw a true image onto a waiting surface.

At home, in her room, she sat at her desk. The bin was full. The form lay in front of her bearing only her name. She understood now. She was not writing a solution to being alive. She was leaving a seed. Not the polished thing. The blue-ink thing she wrote when she thought no one was watching.

But she still could not write it.

She sat a long time. The paper stayed blank. The page waited. In eight million years, if she could find the courage to press her hand to it, a creature that had never heard a voice would find the pressure of her fear, and the pressure would mean something, and the meaning would bloom. That was the promise, and it was also the terror.

She sat until the streetlights dimmed into the small hours. Then she folded the form neatly, the way you fold a flag, and put it back in her planner, and turned off the lamp. She did not sleep well. She dreamed of sunlight falling through a pinhole onto paper, and in the dream the paper was blank, and the light was burning, and a voice that sounded like Whitmore's said: *You have to let it through the hole.*

chapters.name: The Night Before
chapters.content:
By Wednesday night the deadline was a weather system, low and grey and sitting on everything. Amara had gone through the last of her drafts on Tuesday evening, and the flat still smelled faintly of torn paper. The transfer form was folded into her planner, bearing only her name in blue ballpoint, as if the whole message had already been written and the space below were only waiting to be discovered.

Her mother, pulling on her hospice coat for the night shift, had caught her staring at the kitchen wall. "Get out of the house. You've been chewing that pen since I got home. Go and watch the basketball or something." Amara had not argued. Arguing took energy, and she was running on dregs.

So she went to the match.

St. Jude's versus Forest Hill, a Wednesday night in February, the gym as warm as a held breath. The air smelled of floor polish and sweat and Mrs. Abiola's orange squash, fifty pence a cup. The scoreboard said 34–29, but the stands were not watching it; they were watching bodies throw themselves at one another and bounce off, full of heat and purpose. Amara stood by the doors, coat on, cold coming in thin lines around the frame. She had not come to cheer. She had come because her room was full of torn pages and the blank form in her planner glowed like a live wire, and she could not spend another night in the same flat as it.

At half time Callum found her.

He came over with a plastic cup of the orange squash, his satellites trailing, the little constellation of boys who laughed at whatever he said. He stood too close, the way he always did, as if personal space were a rumour. "Okafor. Handed in your poem yet? Train leaves tomorrow."

"Tomorrow's tomorrow," Amara said. It was not a good answer. She felt it failing even as it left her mouth.

Callum smiled like he had won a point. "What's it about, then? Aliens? Eight million years of something." He considered her. "Something from your life. Your dad. The great vanishing act. What's it been, eight years? Not one phone call, my mum says. She says your mum was a mess after he left. Cried at the hospice like she was the patient."

The gym noise seemed to turn down, a hand on a dial. Amara could feel her own face from the inside, a mask she was wearing, and the whole crowd could see through the eyeholes to the thing underneath.

"He left when you were nine," Callum said, tasting the word. "Nine. He looked at his whole life, at you standing in the hallway, and he chose the removals van. You know why?" He didn't wait. "Because you weren't worth coming back for. That's not cruel. That's just the facts. He took one look at you and did the maths."

Her hands were fists. When had that happened? The small moons of her nails pressed into her palms. The heat climbed the back of her skull. A door she had held shut for years was buckling somewhere inside her.

Callum put his face close to hers. "Waste," he said. Quietly. Not shouted, not performed. Stated, like a sum, like something the universe had already settled. "That's your poem, Okafor. That's the whole poem. Waste."

Something in her body made its decision before her mind caught up. It was not a thought; thoughts could be argued with. It was a command from below, from the old part that had kept her alive in the playground, the part that had learned to swallow the word and choke on it. Hit. Swing the school bag. Aim for the mouth. Make him eat it. She saw it happening the way you see a thing through a pinhole—small, distant, perfectly clear: her arm coming up, the weight of the bag, Callum's surprised face, the wet sound, the scramble. In the seeing it became possible.

And then, from a long way off, through the same pinhole, her father's voice spoke the sentence he had spoken on the only day he had ever been completely hers:

*You can't look at it directly. But you can look at what it leaves behind.*

She was nine. Kitchen table. Shoebox. Scissors. Pin. Sunlight falling through foil and throwing a crescent onto white card, small enough to keep, true enough to be the sun. The too-bright thing, made bearable by a hole.

Amara looked at Callum. At the word between them, set down like a dish. Then she turned, pushed the gym door open, and walked out into the cold.

The door closed and the world went quiet. The gym's noise became a muffled animal behind glass. Floodlights poured over the asphalt; the school buildings stood grey and shut. The air was hard with February, the kind of cold that doesn't argue, only waits. Her breath hung in front of her and she stood in the middle of it, shaking.

She wanted to go back. The heat of the almost-fight was still on her skin, the heat of the thing she had almost become. Instead she sat on the steps outside the gym doors. The concrete froze through her jeans. Cold was honest.

She took out the form. The planner, the folded page, her name at the top. The space beneath was white as a frequency.

And she remembered the rest of it.

The shoebox had stayed under her bed for a year after her father left. She used to lift the lid and check the pinhole, the small round emptiness that had let the sun write its true shape. It was proof of a kind: a grocery box, waste, the kind of thing you put out for recycling, could hold a door. Could let the unbearable thing through, and what came through was not fire. It was an image. A print of something too bright to face. Her mother had thrown it out eventually. "Just a box, Amara. It's full of dust." She had cried and could not explain: it was the only lesson her father had left her. You cannot look at the sun. But you can build a small darkness to look through, and the sun will write itself down for you, and you can keep it.

Callum's word was still in the air, a fine grit. *Waste.* The perfect mind's verdict. The playground's verdict. The Ministry of Finance's verdict from the article she had read twice in the library: a project deemed *sentimental waste*. She had been called the word until it was a second name. She had believed it. And when her father left, she had believed it with evidence.

*What the perfect mind calls waste.*

It came to her, the first line, the way a door gives to a shoulder. Not polished. Not pretty. It stood up in the white space and waited.

She uncapped the pen. Bic blue. The same blue as her name. Her hands were shaking—cold, wanting, the aftermath of not swinging. She pressed the pen to the paper.

*What the perfect mind calls waste*

She stopped. It was a confession. *I am that.* The playground, the removals van, the shoebox with its one small hole, the torn drafts in the bin, the girl at the edge of the gym. All of it. The waste. The shelf where the world put what it did not want.

*is the soil where the future blooms.*

It was not a comfort. It was a curse. It was her hand in the air at the back of a perfect mind, saying: you will be outlived by everything you discard. You will pave yourself over and close yourself in, and we will come up through your cracks. She meant it as a confession, and she meant it as a curse, and she did not know, standing in the floodlight spilling from the gym doors, that she had also just left a seed.

She read it twice. A third time, and her eyes blurred, and she looked up at the floodlights until the blur went away.

The card said to give the lines to Mr. Osei, her physics teacher, who would see them to the Lament Archive. But Mr. Osei would keep them in a drawer until morning, and the morning was a lifetime away. If she did not give the lines to Whitmore tonight, she would never again know the shape of what she had written against the dark.

She stood. The paper went into her planner, folded the way you fold a flag. She did not go back through the gym doors. She walked around the science block, footsteps loud in the dead air, and came out through the small gate onto the high street.

A night bus came after ten minutes, a lit box of winter. She sat at the back. The windows were streaked with someone else's rain. Shops shut, takeaways open, the sodium lights making the streets the colour of tea. A woman in a hospital lanyard slept across the aisle with her mouth open, and Amara thought of her mother in her hospice coat, holding a hand through the dark, watching people finish. *There is no part of it you get to keep.* Whitmore had said that. She was beginning to understand.

She got off at the bottom of the hill and climbed. The observatory was a dark mass against the sky, the white dome like a skull. The public doors were locked; the visitors were long gone. But a light burned in a corner window on the first floor—Whitmore's corner, the one over the park. His light burned late.

The side door was unlocked, as it had been on Tuesday. She let herself in. The corridor smelled of old paper and floor polish and the unshakeable cold inside old buildings. She climbed slowly, so her footsteps would not echo, and knocked on the office door. There was a long pause, a slow scrape of a chair, and then the door opened.

Elias Whitmore looked smaller than he had on Tuesday, if that was possible. He wore his navy coat, collar up. His hands shook at his sides. He looked at her, then at the planner in her hands, and did not ask why she was there.

"You wrote it," he said. It was not a question.

"Yes."

He stood aside. The office was the same museum of him: stacks of paper, soldered wire, a cold cup of tea, the scale model of the Lament on the filing cabinet, gold foil catching the lamp light. She took out the form and held it out. Her hand was red from the cold. The paper was cold too; it was the only living thing in the room for a moment.

He took it in both hands to steady them. The blue ink had dried quickly in the freezing air. She knew the two lines by heart; she had stitched them to herself on the way over, and now the paper carried them away and she felt the stitching tear.

Whitmore read it.

He read it again.

The clock ticked. Two. Three. Five. In the lamp light, the blue ink was the blue of the sky over Lewisham just after the streetlights give up. The words were not printed. They were pressed—a fossil of a body. A light passing through a small hole.

Whitmore set the paper down with the slowness of a man handling something that could break. His hands had stopped shaking. He looked past her, out at the dark over the park.

Then he said, "You have no idea what you've sent into the dark."

Amara stood very still. "Is it the right thing?"

Whitmore picked the page up and read the lines again, his lips moving over the words the way you'd touch a raised scar. "It's not good, Amara. And it's not right. It's true. That's a different contract." He set it down, aligning it with the edge of the desk. "You think you've written a curse. You've written a key. You think you've written a confession. You've written a door." He looked at her. "Let it close."

"I don't—"

"You will. That's the bargain." His voice was thicker than usual, but his hands lay still on either side of the page. "You'll carry the not-knowing for the rest of your life. You'll wonder if it was enough. You'll remember a girl outside a gym with a blue pen, and you'll believe she was a waste, and the paper will be out there, past the orbits, still saying what she was too afraid to say out loud." He set his hands flat. "That's the cart and the push. That's the whole engine. The not-knowing."

She wanted to take the paper back. She could feel it leaving her, the way the crescent had faded from the white card when her father packed away the shoebox. But it was not hers. It had not been hers since the ink dried.

At the door she turned. The model of the Lament caught the lamplight, absurdly bright, its dish angled toward the ceiling that stood, in the model's small universe, for a sky without end. Whitmore was already reading the lines again, bent over the page like a man sheltering a match from the wind. She closed the door very quietly and left him there, learning the words by heart, as if he had waited his whole life for a name.

She walked down the hill through the cold. The lines were no longer in her planner. They were on a desk in a lit window, and then they were not even there; they were traveling, already traveling, though she could not feel the motion. She would eat toast in the morning and go to school. The blank would be filled, and the filled thing would be gone, and she would spend the rest of her life trying to remember exactly what it had felt like to press the pen down in the floodlight, with the word still ringing in her ears, the cold coming up through the concrete, and mean it.

chapters.name: Launch from Cornwall
chapters.content:
# 4. Launch from Cornwall

The coach left London at half past eleven on the night of the thirteenth of May, which Amara had always thought of as the hour for people who were either going somewhere or not coming back. She had a seat to herself at the back, a packed lunch her mother had made before the night shift, and the kind of headache that comes from not having slept at all. The other passengers were mostly adults in fleeces carrying press passes and binoculars. Near the front, a teacher she didn't recognise was already asleep with her mouth open. The only other person under thirty was Dev Patel, who boarded at the last stop with a paperback and a can of something and paused at her row as if he had been looking for her.

"You came," Amara said.

"You're the one who wrote it. I'm just here to see whether it melts on the way up." He dropped into the seat across the aisle. "Also my geography teacher said I could get coursework out of it."

"'The Lament Archive: a case study in strategic cultural investment.'"

"Something like that." He looked at her for a moment, not unkindly. "You don't have to talk to me."

"Okay."

"Okay."

The coach pulled out of the station and the dark city began to slide past the windows. Three months, Amara thought. Three months since the gym steps, since the blue pen, since she had stood in Whitmore's lit office and watched his hands stop shaking over two lines she had written as a confession and a curse. The couplet had been entered into the archive — folded into the Lament's payload manifest under a number she hadn't asked for — and once it was sealed she had stopped being able to feel it, like a limb that has gone to sleep. It was like a stone dropped into a deep well: you know it is falling, but after a time the falling ceases to have an image. You only know the well is deep because you no longer hear it land.

The letter from Whitmore had come in the second week of May, in the sloping hand she had learned to recognise. *Launch window confirmed. 14 May, 05:47, Cornwall. The page is in — canister three. You should be there. You wrote it.*

Her mother had asked whether she should take the night off. Amara had said no before the question had fully landed.

"It's just a rocket."

Her mother had looked at her with that long, exhausted attention, the way she looked at patients trying to tell her something they didn't have words for, and then she had nodded. "You'll tell me about it when you're back."

"Yes."

But they both knew she wouldn't. Telling her mother things had once meant telling her father things, in the kitchen of the old flat, and look where that had got her. She had never told her mother what she had written. The words were no longer hers to say.

Cornwall arrived in the dark, in a smell of cold sea and wet grass that came through the vents like a change of weather. The launch site was a field above the cliffs outside Newquay, floodlit until it hummed, covered in marquees and portable toilets and people with cameras you could have used as walking sticks. Beyond the wire fence, out over the dark water, the rocket stood on its pad: a white needle threaded with floodlights, so bright against the black that it looked printed rather than physical. Amara walked to the fence with the other passengers and stood in the wind, her hands in her pockets. The wind came off the sea in a steady pressure, smelling of salt and the peculiar emptiness of places that exist only for leaving.

It was impossible that anything she had written was inside that.

Whitmore found her before the light came up. He was walking with a stick now; the navy coat had shrunk around him, or he had shrunk inside it. His voice had a thickness at the edges, as if the words were climbing a small hill before they could leave him. But his eyes, grey as the winter sky she remembered, grey as the sea beyond the pad, found her and held her.

"There you are," he said, like he had been looking for her a long time.

She wanted to say something fine. She said, "You've got a stick."

"Souvenir." He leaned on it. "Come and see the model."

He led her to a marquee where the project's engineers stood around a thermos, and there on the trestle table stood the Lament. Not the real one. A cardboard replica the size of a small suitcase, made of corrugated box and silver foil and the excellent intentions of a Year 8 design class. It was gloriously, heartbreakingly wonky. The dish antenna leaned like a sunflower after rain. LAMENT was written on the side in marker pen, with a full stop after it, as if the word were a sentence and had been finished.

"Mrs Abiola's form made it," Whitmore said, almost tenderly. "I thought the photograph might like it."

"The photograph?"

"The newspaper. They want a picture of the poet and the scientist." He smiled his crooked smile. "You and me. With the stand-in."

So that was the job. Amara picked up the cardboard Lament. It was absurdly light, lighter than a shoebox, and for a second she was nine years old again, holding her father's pinhole projector — proof that a grocery box could let the unbearable thing through as an image rather than fire. The memory came and went like a cold draught. She looked out at the rocket on the pad and thought of the real Lament folded inside it like a seed in a pod, carrying soil from six continents, and the sounds of a world that would be mostly gone before it returned, and her two lines of blue ink.

"Is it really in there?" she asked.

"Canister three." Whitmore said it as if it were the answer to a question she hadn't been able to ask. "I put it in myself. The last page. It went in after the seeds, the soil, the sounds. I wanted it on top."

"Why?"

"Because it was the thing I wanted to find."

The dawn came up out of the Atlantic like a held breath being let go. It began as a seam of grey at the horizon, wide and patient, and then it widened into apricot, into gold, and the light ran across the water in a straight line to the cliff, as if the sun had an appointment with this particular piece of coast. The floodlights went off. The rocket appeared suddenly as a white tower against a pale sky, and a voice on the tannoy began counting the things a machine must know before it lets go of something it has built.

The photographer found them in the gold light, a small man with a large camera and the air of one who had photographed many things leaving. He arranged them against the fence with the sea behind them and the rocket in the background, and asked Amara to hold the cardboard model.

"Just stand beside him, love. Yes. And can you look at the model like it's the real one?"

She looked down at the cardboard Lament, at the wonky dish, at the full stop after LAMENT. She looked at the rocket on the pad, still white against the pale sky, and thought of the Lament folded inside it, waiting for the moment it would begin to fall. Eight million years of falling. That was what the future was: a long curve that began with a push.

"Like you're looking at something beautiful," the photographer said.

She looked up, into the lens, and she smiled. She actually smiled. It was the strangest feeling, stranger than crying: as if the smile had been borrowed from the girl she would become in the photograph, the girl in the newspaper, the girl who was, for one glittering second, visible. The flash went off. The moment was sealed into light.

Whitmore shook the photographer's hand. "Thank you."

"Pleasure." The photographer lowered the camera and seemed, for a second, genuinely moved. "The girl and the old man, holding the cardboard thing with the real thing behind them. That's a proper photograph, that is."

Then the countdown began, and the moment of being looked at was over. The tannoy counted down from ten. Amara stood at the fence gripping the wire, the cardboard Lament jammed under one arm, and felt her heart — which she had always thought of as a night-shift worker, a quiet organ keeping the lights on — begin to gallop. Whitmore stood at her shoulder. She thought she heard him stop breathing. Somewhere behind them a woman was crying, a sound that could almost have been laughter, and no one laughed.

Then the rocket lit.

Light came first, a whiteness that erased the idea of shadow and turned the sea to brass and the gorse to black lines on the hill. Then the sound reached them, not as noise but as weather, a physical press on the chest that sank into the bones of the earth. It was like standing inside a storm and being allowed to survive it. The rocket did not climb so much as the ground became too small to hold it, and it went up trailing a plume of fire that lengthened and lengthened, and the sound kept arriving, a roar that after a while stopped being a sound and became a presence.

Amara did not know she was crying until she tasted salt. Her face was simply running, the way the sky runs when it cannot help itself. The rocket was high now, a white dot with a comet's tail, and the crowd broke into applause — that strange clapping at things that are leaving, as if welcoming them home.

Whitmore touched her elbow. His hand was shaking, but his eyes were dry and very bright.

"There it goes," he said. "Eight million years."

She could not speak. The rocket was a star now, falling upward. She watched until it went out, or until the sky swallowed it. The sun was fully up. The sky was pale blue and empty. The sea was empty too, and the pad where the rocket had stood was just a pad, a shape with nothing inside it.

The silence came down like a weight. All that sound had been a kind of violence, and the absence of it was a second violence, deeper. She stood with the wire cutting into her hands and understood that the not-knowing had begun in earnest. Somewhere above her the Lament was already turning toward Mars, toward the long curve that would take eight million years to complete, and every second the distance grew, and there was nothing she could do but stand on the grass and be gone from it.

"What happens to it now?" she asked.

"It falls." Whitmore's voice was slow, the words climbing their small hill. "It falls past Mars, and Jupiter bends it, and Saturn bends it, and Neptune lets it go out past the Kuiper belt, and the gravity of the long curve turns it around and brings it back. Eight million years of falling." He looked at her. "You don't aim a thing like that. You let it go."

They walked back through the marquees in the new light. Engineers shook Whitmore's hand; he let them, smiling in a way she had not seen him smile before. Amara stood to one side with the cardboard Lament in her arms, pleased and not pleased, visible and not visible, trying to hold onto the feeling of the flash. For one hour she was happy — a plain, physical fact, like being warm. She knew it would not last. She let it.

Dev found her leaning against a marquee pole, watching the empty sky.

"You cried," he said.

"You'll put that in your coursework."

"Yeah." He leaned beside her. "Except I don't think I'll be able to say what I want to. 'Lament launch: a girl cried over a cardboard satellite. If she hadn't, we'd be in trouble.'" He shrugged. "Doesn't fit the word count."

It was the kindest thing anyone had said to her since February.

The coach left Cornwall at midday, in the flat white light of an afternoon that felt as if the morning had never happened. Amara sat by the window with the cardboard Lament on her knees. The sea went past, and the fields, and the towns, and then the city took her back, grey and low and ordinary. When she got home her mother was asleep — night shift — and Amara stood in the kitchen eating toast that tasted of nothing, then put the cardboard model on the shelf above her desk, where it could watch her revise. She left the packed lunch, untouched, in the fridge. She typed a message to her mother — *It went up.* — and sent it, knowing it would sit on the bedside table through the evening, unopened, waiting, like something sealed in a canister.

That night she lay in the dark and thought of the real Lament, moving through a darkness much larger than hers, beyond the Moon's orbit, on its way to the gravity of Jupiter. Whatever was there when it returned would not be her species. It might not read her words in any language that existed now. But the pages were there, the blue ink was there, the pressure of her hand held in the groove of the letters, sealed under noble gas in the dark.

*What the perfect mind calls waste*
*is the soil where the future blooms.*

She had not spoken the lines aloud since the night she wrote them. She moved her mouth in the dark, and the words came back the way a note comes back when a piano is opened, and she lay listening to them settle into the shape of a door.

Sometime in the small hours she slept. And the satellite, which had no need of sleep, continued its long falling curve through the outer dark. It carried seeds no perfect mind had seen any use for, soil from fields ploughed by hands now dust, six hundred voices speaking languages that would die before it rounded its first bend, and her couplet — two lines of blue ink on a sheet of cellulose, all that was left of a girl on a cold night, all that would ever be found of her. It travelled in a silence so complete that any perfect mind would have called it emptiness. But it was not empty. It was moving, full of the thing it had been asked to keep, and it would still be moving in eight million years, when the Earth it was returning to would be waiting or would not — and either way it would arrive.

chapters.name: Visible
chapters.content:
# Visible

The day after the launch was the longest Friday of Amara's life.

She woke before the alarm, and for a moment the flat was exactly as it had always been—grey light at the curtain, the radiator ticking, the smell of her mother's night shift lingering in the corridor like a thing that had not yet left. Then she turned her head and saw the cardboard Lament on the shelf above her desk, the leaning dish antenna, the full stop after LAMENT, and the whole of Thursday came back like weather moving over a field. The rocket. The light that had erased shadow. The photograph, still only light, trapped in a camera, waiting to become a thing.

She went to school.
