The world had got up and put on the same grey clothes and expected her to do the same, and nothing had changed: the corridors, the lost-property box, the smell of floor polish and cold toast. The Lament was gone, but the school had not noticed its going. At lunch she sat in the library annex and watched the ordinary weather of the year pass. Nobody looked at her. Nobody had seen the photograph. She was invisible in the old, comfortable way, and she had not known until that Friday how much the visibility of Thursday had meant—the one hour of happiness, a plain physical fact, like being warm, now packed away like the packed lunch left uneaten in the fridge.

Dev Patel passed her in the corridor after last period. He did not stop. "You'll be in the paper," he said, without looking at her. "Mark my words." Then he was gone, and Amara stood in the stream of students with her heart beating far too hard for the size of the sentence.

---

The paper came on Saturday.

Her mother was sitting at the kitchen table when Amara came down, still in her coat from the night shift, too tired to go to bed, the way she got sometimes—too tired to do anything but sit and let the tiredness settle. The newspaper was open in front of her. The kettle was cold. The paper had been open long enough that the pages had curved, the way things curve when they are left too long in one shape.

"Amara," her mother said. Not a question. A summons.

Amara came to the table. Her mother turned the paper around.

It was the South London Press, page three. And there was the photograph—the girl and the old man, holding the cardboard thing with the real thing behind them. The dawn light was the colour of apricots. The rocket stood behind them like a promise the size of a needle. And there was Amara's face, wearing a smile she did not remember choosing, the smile of the girl she had become in the moment before the flash: visible, glittering, real.

The headline said: LEWISHAM STUDENT'S POEM SET FOR EIGHT-MILLION-YEAR VOYAGE. The caption named her. The article was short—four paragraphs, a quote from Whitmore about a message in a bottle to the deep future, a quote from the headteacher about the school being immensely proud—and then, in the third paragraph, printed in black type far too small for the thing it was carrying, were the two lines she had written on a cold night with a blue Bic on a form she had nearly torn up.

Her mother read them aloud. Her voice was rough from the shift—the voice of a woman who had spent the night watching people breathe their last—and it made the lines sound the way they had sounded on the gym steps: not like poetry, but like a thing a person says when they have been pushed to the edge of what they can carry.

"What the perfect mind calls waste / is the soil where the future blooms."

The kitchen was very quiet. The fridge hummed its one tired note; the clock did its arithmetic.

"You wrote this," her mother said. Not a question.

"Yes."

"You never told me."

"I didn't know how." Amara heard the sentence and knew it was true, and not enough, and everything. "I didn't know it would be in the paper. He said the words were no longer mine to say."

Her mother looked at the photograph for a long time. Her finger came up and touched the glass of her daughter's smile. "That's you," she said. "That's really you."

Amara stood very still. Her mother had seen her. Not the invisible girl. Not the girl who was "asked to" write something for a satellite. Her. The one who wrote the thing. The one in the light.

Then her mother did a strange thing. She took the paper to the drawer where the kitchen scissors lived, and cut the whole page out—photograph, headline, article, the couplet—with the slow, focused attention of a woman who had learned to make things last. She folded it into four squares, pressed the creases flat with the heel of her hand, and put it into the breast pocket of her coat, over her heart.

"I want to show them at the hospice," she said. "Dr. Mensah. The nurses." She paused, and the tiredness on her face became something else. "We see a lot of waste in that place. That's what they call it. Old people, dying people, people who can't do anything anymore, and the paperwork calls it waste. But the ones who stay—the ones who sit with it, who hold a hand through the night, you should see what grows out of that." She looked at Amara with something that was almost light. "You wrote it down. I've been living it for twenty years and I never knew how to say it. You wrote it down."

She said it as if Amara had built her a house.

Amara's eyes stung. She did not let them spill. But she stood at her own kitchen table and let the pride of her mother move through her—small, exhausted, blazing, like a match in a storm—and thought: this is being seen.

Her mother's phone was on the table. She picked it up, thumbed the screen, and read aloud: "'It went up.'" She looked at Amara. "I read it this morning. Before the paper. I saw it and I thought, she means the rocket. And then I opened the paper." She put the phone down. "It went up," she said again, softly—and Amara understood she was not talking about the rocket anymore.

---

The weekend shimmered. There was no other word for it. The grey had been washed out of the sky and the light given one extra degree of brightness, so that everything it touched looked newly made. Amara's phone began to buzz—her phone, which normally sat at the bottom of her bag like a stone in a streambed. Classmates had found her number and were sending her things: a thumbs-up, a rocket emoji, a screenshot of the article, "That's you!!", "I didn't know you wrote poems." She answered with small, cautious replies—"thanks," "yeah"—and felt the strangeness of the new shape she was wearing, like a coat that had not yet worn in.

Mrs. Abiola's Year 8 form had seen the photograph. On Saturday afternoon a message arrived from a number she did not know: "hi miss we made the model!!! ur holding our model!!! its in the paper!!!" followed by a blur of peace signs. Amara laughed out loud in the empty flat, a real laugh, from somewhere deep that had been boarded up.

The cardboard Lament sat on the shelf above her desk, and she looked at it with new eyes. It had been in the paper. It had been held up at dawn with the real thing behind it, and the real thing was still falling, and the stand-in was here, watching her revise—both of them waste, and both of them throwing a true image onto a waiting surface, the way the shoebox had once thrown a crescent of light onto a page. You can't look at it directly, her father had said. But you can look at what it leaves behind.

---

On Sunday morning Whitmore called her. It was the first time he had ever telephoned her, and his voice was thicker than she remembered—the words climbing their small hill.

"Come to the observatory. There's something I want to show you. A thing about the trajectory. You should see where your words are going."

He was waiting at the gate, leaning on his stick in the same navy coat, and for a moment he looked like a man who had been waiting there for months—as if the launch had taken from him whatever had been holding him upright. But his eyes were bright. He took her up to the corner office, the room where she had delivered her draft in February, and it was stripped: the books boxed, the posters rolled, the desk bare except for a dark tube leaning against the wall.

"You're moving," Amara said.

"Retiring," said Whitmore. "As of Friday. The project is over. There is nothing left for me to do here except be an old man taking up space." He said it without bitterness, like a man reciting a fact about the weather. Then he unrolled the tube.

A sheet of dark paper, printed with the solar system. A trajectory plot, made for the archive: a long thin gold line arcing across the black like a single stroke of calligraphy written by a hand told not to hurry. Earth, a small blue dot. Mars. Jupiter—the line bent, unhurried. Saturn—another bend, graceful. Neptune, and then the line ran straight and clean out past a dotted boundary labelled KUIPER BELT, into a region where there were no more labels, only stars—and then it began to curve.

"Eight million years," Whitmore said, tracing the path with a fingertip that shook. "The slingshots. The long fall. The bend that turns it around and brings it home." The returning arc was a gold comma, a question that had gone to the edge of the answer and decided to come back. "Here is where it will be when it passes Earth again. Eight million years from now. It will not slow down. It will not wait for an answer. It is a message arriving at a house that may or may not still be standing, and the message does not care if the house is there. The message will simply be."

"Is it still going?" she asked. It was a stupid question. She could not stop it.

Whitmore smiled—the launch smile, the one that did not belong to the tired voice or the failing hands. "It is still going. Right now, while you are standing here. It will be going when I am ash and you are old and every building in this city is dust. It will be going when they have built cities over this one, and forgotten them, and built again. It is still going, Amara. That is the only thing I can promise you."

He was quiet. Then the brightness in his eyes became something careful, almost regretful.

"Which is why I must tell you something you will not want to hear."

Amara waited. The air in the room changed, the way it changes before weather.

"There are people who will not forgive this." He gestured at the gold line. "The Ministry of Finance called the Lament sentimental waste before it launched. They will call it worse now. They will call it a waste of money, a waste of your talents, a waste of the years you could have spent doing something measurable. And they will call you—" he put his hand on the desk to steady it—"the beautiful waste at the centre of it. The girl who wrote a poem when she should have been revising."

"Waste," Amara said. The word was old and familiar in her mouth, like a tooth she had been born with.

"Yes." Whitmore looked at her steadily. "The world may not forgive a beautiful waste. Not because the world is cruel—though it is—but because the world is efficient. Efficiency cannot read a poem. It looks at a thing that cannot be measured and calls it nothing, and files it away, and the filing is so thorough that the thing becomes genuinely hard to find. They will try to file this away, Amara. They will try to file you away. And they will do it thoroughly."

Amara stood very still. The gold line was still on the paper. The words were still in canister three. That had not changed. That would never change.

"Is that what's going to happen?" she asked.

"I don't know," said Whitmore. "I know the satellite does not care. I know the words are already out there, falling. I know that whether or not the world forgives them, they will arrive. I wanted you to see the line so that when they tell you it was all waste, you will remember it is also still going." He touched the gold curve again, very gently, like a man touching a thing he had loved. "That is the hope, Amara. Not that they will forgive you. That they will not be able to stop it. The words are out of their hands. They are out of yours too. They are out where the perfect mind calls nothing, and they are still going."

---

Amara walked home from Greenwich in the long Sunday light, the trajectory printed on the inside of her eyelids. She did not take the bus. She walked down the hill through the park, the city spread out below her like a thing laid down to sleep.

She thought about February, the cold steps, the blue pen. She had meant the couplet as a confession and a curse: she was the waste, and the perfect mind would be outlived by everything it discarded. But Whitmore had said she had written a door. She had written a key. And now, standing on the bridge with the river glittering below, she began to understand the difference.

Hope had always been the thing that made the falling worse. Hope was what you had when you were nine, checking the window for a van that had already gone. Hope was the hour of sleep you lost waiting for a reply that had never come. She had learned to distrust it—the bright child's balloon of a thing, always rising, always coming down.

But this hope was quieter. It was a seed's hope. It did not need to know where the soil was. It only needed to be planted.

When she got home, her mother was asleep, and the flat was full of the particular stillness of a body resting after a night of carrying other people's deaths. Amara went to her desk. The cardboard Lament was on the shelf—the wonky dish, the full stop, the foil that had caught the dawn light and the flash of the camera and the colour printing of the paper, all in the same small act of standing in for something real. She touched the dish antenna and watched it lean back.

"What the perfect mind calls waste," she said aloud, to the empty flat, to the cardboard, to the dark beyond the window, "is the soil where the future blooms."

The words went out into the air. She did not know where they went. But she knew, with a certainty she had never felt before, that they were still going—that they would be going when she was ash and the buildings were dust and the grey city had become geology, going whether the world forgave them or not.

On Monday the headteacher would announce it over the tannoy, and the classroom would turn to look at her in one slow motion, and Callum would walk past her table with his face a closed door, and Dev would sit down in the library annex and tell her the poem was the kind of not-bad that made you think oh, that's what everyone's been trying to say, and she would count the floor tiles to hold herself steady, and the gold line would still be falling behind every moment of it.

She did not know if anyone would ever read her words.

She began to hope anyway.

That was the whole of it. She began to hope anyway.

chapters.name: The Shape of Efficiency
chapters.content:
# The Shape of Efficiency

"Hope is a budget." Praetor Lenore Voss said it on the evening broadcast in the flat grey way of a woman reading a weather report, and half the world believed her. She stood at a lectern shaped like a single held line, with the Concord's emblem behind her—a horizon, held level—and she spoke of the Long Crises as if they had been a leak. The bad harvests. The steel shortages. The three pandemics that had closed the schools of England twice and the coasts of the world three times. The children migrating inland like tide-driven things. "A civilization that hopes in every direction starves in every direction," she said. "We will allocate hope. We will spend it where it grows."

Amara was nineteen, sitting in the refectory at the University of Greenwich with an empty cup and an open astronomy textbook, watching the screen above the till like everyone else. Two years to the week since the launch. The Lament had been gone two years, and she had spent those years learning the grammar of the thing she had sent—orbital mechanics, perturbation theory, the long patience of gravity. She wanted to understand what the gold line was doing out there, even if she could not see it. The cardboard Lament still sat on her desk in the room she rented by the river, foil dented, the dish antenna leaning like a sunflower after rain, LAMENT finished with the full stop Mrs Abiola's Year 8 form had given it, as if the word were a sentence and had been completed. The future she had trusted was a line, and the line was still going. She recited the couplet aloud in the small hours, the way other girls her age recited song lyrics. It had become a fixture of the interior. She did not know it was about to be made a fixture of something else.

The Concord's lettering reached the corridors before the end of term. A poster appeared during exam week, grey sans-serif on white: NOTHING SPENT ON NOTHING. Beneath it, smaller: *Hope is a budget. Spend it where it grows.* Amara stood before it with her books pressed against her chest and read it twice. It was a poem, she realized—an efficiency report that had accidentally grown a metaphor. Voss spoke of hope the way the Ministry of Finance had spoken of the Lament: as a resource, an account, a thing that could run dry. The only difference was that Voss had given the word *waste* an architecture.

It began, as such things do, with what could be measured. A memo from the new office of Civic Efficiency asked departments to list activities without demonstrable civic return. The astronomy department's public open evening—the one where Amara had stood at a table showing schoolchildren how to make a pinhole projector from a shoebox, teaching them that you cannot look at an eclipse directly but you can look at what it leaves behind—was cancelled within the week. "Unproductive sentiment," the memo said. Amara read the phrase on the departmental notice board and felt it enter her like a stone entering water. That was what her father's shoebox was called in the new official language. That was what her father had taught her in the year before the removals van came. Unproductive sentiment.

She wrote to the office of Civic Efficiency. She did not expect an answer, and she did not receive one. She drafted a second letter, five hundred words of careful argument about the measurable returns of wonder, and left it on her desk beside the cardboard Lament, unsent. Something about the Concord's calm made sending things feel like a form of kneeling.

The recruitment table appeared at the edge of the covered market in the last week of May. A grey booth, a levelled horizon, volunteers in clean shirts offering pamphlets: TRAIN IN HOPE ALLOCATION. The Administrative Corps, the pamphlet explained, would staff the allocation offices and the cultural efficiency review and the new ministries. *Learn to decide what matters.* Amara stood at a distance reading it, the word *matters* sitting oddly in her mouth, and then someone said her name.

Dev Patel was leaning on the barrier beside the booth with a pamphlet folded in his back pocket. He was twenty, built straighter somehow, still wearing the same orange jacket he had worn to the launch, older now in the shoulders and the careful way he held himself. He looked at her with the old almost-kindness.

"I thought you'd be on the list," he said. "Volunteering."

Amara shook her head. "I write letters. They don't answer them."

"They answered mine," Dev said. "Three times. They wanted to know why I'd gone to Cornwall overnight." He shrugged. "They file everything, Okafor. That's the thing about them. Nothing gets burned. It just gets put somewhere deep."

He described the allocation logic with a terrible, gentle fluency. The dialysis machine reallocated to his mother's ward. The flood defence on the Thames. The childhood leukaemia research that had been waiting twelve years for funding and finally had it. "The Lament can't do any of that, Amara. It's beautiful. It was the kind of not-bad—" he stopped, smiled, remembering the library annex, the corridor, the girl who had cried over a cardboard satellite. "It's what everyone's been trying to say. I still mean it. But it can't do that."

"It doesn't have to," Amara said. "It isn't the same kind of thing. That's the whole point. It doesn't compete with the dialysis machine. It's the reason anyone on that ward bothers to want a dialysis machine to exist."

Dev looked at her for a long moment. Then he said, quietly, "Eight million years is a long time to wait for a return you'll never receive."

"Seeds take time," Amara said. "You put them in the ground and the ground does the rest, and the tree that comes up—" She stopped. She could hear Whitmore in the echo, and the echo made her chest ache. "You'll see, Dev. They'll file the Lament. It'll still be going."

"They've already filed it," he said. "It's in the interim report. Under unproductive sentiment. They quote your poem, Amara. They had to write it down to ban it."

He pulled a folded grey document from the pocket beneath the pamphlet and handed it to her. THE SHAPE OF EFFICIENCY: INTERIM REPORT OF THE CULTURAL ALLOCATION REVIEW. The cover was the colour of wet pavements. A levelled line. *Prepared for the Ministry of Cultural Efficiency.*

Page four, under *Programmes identified as unproductive sentiment*, she found the Lament Archive between a national poetry curriculum and a database of endangered dialects: *deep-space time capsule; projected return on investment: absent; completion status: achieved; recommendation: records reclassified, no further allocation.* And in a footnote, as if it were evidence:

*Project message (student), quoted in full: "What the perfect mind calls waste / is the soil where the future blooms." — A. Okafor, age 17.*

She had to stop and breathe. The words had been hers. Now they were an exhibit. The poem she had written so that it would outlive the world had been made Exhibit A by the world.

She found Whitmore in Catford that evening, in the top-floor flat he had moved to a year earlier *because it has a wall for the plot and a landlord who doesn't mind a dying man taking up space*. The trajectory plot was pinned above the gas fire—dark paper, the long gold line arcing past Mars, Jupiter bending it unhurried, Saturn bending it graceful, the comma at the edge of the answer deciding to come back. It was the first thing she saw when he opened the door. The second was the walking frame, and the cane hanging from the arm of the chair, and the way his right hand lay curled on the armrest like a bird that had decided not to fly again.

He was thinner. The navy coat that had shrunk around him now hung from him in folds, and his voice had thickened further. But his eyes were the same: bright, exact, amused at the wrong time.

"You've seen it," he said. "The shape of efficiency. Very well named. It is the most efficient document ever written. It does the work of a bonfire without burning a single page."

Amara unfolded the grey cover. He watched her find the entry and read it, and his face did not change. She read her own words in the footnote and felt them go down into her like cold water.

"They had to write it down," Whitmore said, "in order to file it. They have memorized your couplet to bury it. Don't be comforted by that." His voice softened. "But don't be entirely un-comforted, either."

"How are the letters?" she asked.

"Forty-six written. Two answered. The answers are efficient." He said it without bitterness, as if it were a result he had calculated and was not displeased with. "I asked them to preserve the Archive as a historical record. They declined. The Archive will be reclassified as waste, which is—" he gestured with his good hand, a small ceremony of emphasis, "—the truer filing. Do you understand, Amara? They think they are putting it in a bin. They are putting it in the ground."

She did not answer. She folded the report and put it in the pocket of her coat, over her heart, where her mother kept the newspaper cutting. She had her own cutting now, folded into four squares, pressed flat, taken from the wall of her room in Lewisham when she moved to Greenwich. She did not know why she carried it. She only knew it was the kind of thing Whitmore would call a cart.

"They have cut the telemetry budget," he said. "There is nothing to receive anyway; the ephemeris is complete. The orbit is a written sentence, and it is finished." He paused. "They closed the last door they could close. It is the most hopeful thing they have done."

Amara looked at the plot. The gold line, written by a hand told not to hurry. "It's Tuesday, isn't it," she said. She had the calculations in her head; she had been counting down without admitting it.

"The first bend," Whitmore said. "Mars. 04:12 in the morning. It will not slow down and it will not ask permission. The gravitational field will bend its path, and the bending will make this whole efficient Concord a smaller and smaller part of the shape of it." He tapped the gold line where it passed the red dot. "I tried to book us time at the observatory. We have been refused. Observing time, they explained, is allocated by demonstrated output." He smiled, and for a moment he looked like the man who had stood in the prep room handing her a pair of binoculars as if they were the keys to a kingdom. "So I will sit here, at 04:12, in this chair, and I will watch the air where the gold line is. And I want you to do the same, from wherever you are. So that there is a witness."

"A witness without a sight line," Amara said.

Whitmore's eyes lit. "That is faith, Amara. A witness without a sight line. A seed is a witness without a sight line. It does not know where the soil is. It only knows it has been planted."

His right hand uncurled an inch and then curled again. Amara watched the effort travel down his wrist and fail at the knuckles. She did not offer to help, and he did not ask. The kettle came up slowly, in two hands, and he poured the tea with an exaggerated ceremony, as if the pouring were a form of defiance.

"One more thing," he said. "Don't spend your twenties writing letters to people who file them." He looked at her over the cup, which was steady between both palms. "I spent a decade writing letters to rooms that were never occupied. You wrote something that didn't need a room. Let them file the letters for both of us."

She took the 47 back through Lewisham with the report over her heart. The bus went past the turn for the old school, past the library, past streets she had counted on the night of the draft that became the poem. Her mother had texted during the afternoon: *They've given the word a column.* St Christopher's had new paperwork now, a form that asked nurses to classify patients by projected recovery. Waste was one of the options. Her mother had not said anything more. She had not needed to.

Tuesday began at 04:12. Amara was not at her desk; she had left the room at half past three and walked up through Greenwich Park, past the sleeping chestnuts and the closed gates, to the hill where the observatory stood. The dome was dark. A new notice had been fixed to the iron gate: SCHEDULED OBSERVING — AUTHORISED PERSONNEL & DEMONSTRATED OUTPUT ONLY. She did not try the gate. She stood on the path above the sleeping city, under the tilted dark, and looked at the sky where the calculations said the Lament was passing Mars.

She could not see it. She had known she would not see it. There was the red point of Mars, faint through the haze—or she believed there was; the city ate the sky with yellow light. The Lament was out there, smaller than the cardboard one on her desk, falling at the speed of a thing that had decided not to hurry. Mars was bending it. The first bend. Eight million years had already begun; the question had gone out to the edge of the answer and was beginning, for the first time, to consider coming back.

She said the couplet aloud. The first time, it was the curse she had meant it to be. The second time, it was the key Whitmore had said it was. She stood in the dark with a grey report folded over her heart and her own words in her mouth, and understood all at once what he had meant: the world was closing the door, but the door had never been the thing she trusted. The future she had trusted was a line on dark paper, a gold comma falling past a red world, invisible to every witness, bending around the gravity of so much unproductive sentiment. Let them file it. Let them call it waste. The bin had become the ground.

She stood on the hill until the sky began to grey, then walked down through the empty park toward the river, the hill behind her like a closed door she had refused to knock on. She had not seen it. She had not needed to see it. Somewhere above the breathing city, past the haze and the yellow light, a gold line was bending around a red world, carrying soil, seeds, six hundred dying voices, and a girl who had believed she was writing a curse.

They could call it waste until the sun went out.

They could not stop it being planted.

chapters.name: The Ministry of Cultural Efficiency
chapters.content:
The hearing notice was the size of a postcard and the weight of a door.

Amara found it in her student pigeonhole in the last week of November, six months after the first bend at Mars. It was printed on Ministry paper, grey, with nothing wasted on it. At the top, the levelled horizon. Below it: *In the matter of the Cultural Allocation Review: Programme Lament Archive. A determination hearing will convene. The project lead is invited to make representations. Students of relevant departments may apply to observe in a non-speaking capacity.*

She called Whitmore from the payphone in the corridor. His voice was thinner than it had been in spring, but the old amusement was still in it.

"They've given me a hearing."

"Are you going to go?"

"I'm going. I've been invited to make representations. I'm going to represent the seeds." A pause, a shift against the chair. "But I want you there. I want a witness without a sight line."

"I'll be there."

The hearing convened on a Tuesday in Room 14 of the Ministry of Cultural Efficiency, in a building on Belvedere Road that had once sold curtains. Grey cord carpet swallowed every footstep, so the room felt like a held breath. A long table. A water jug. A stack of forms. Observers' chairs against the wall, facing the table as you might face a wall. Amara had brought the grey interim report, folded in her coat pocket, over her heart, as though a thing that was going to be harmed ought to have a witness to the harm before the harm was done again.

At the side table stood Dev Patel in the uniform of the new Administrative Corps, the levelled horizon at his collar. A case file lay closed before him. When she came in his face did something complicated and then settled. He raised four fingers, a small wave, and put his hand where it could not be seen.

The panel entered. Chief Examiner Vell had grey hair pulled back tight and glasses that made her eyes the size of the printed code on her desk. Two assessors sat with her, one holding a pen, one with a finger following clauses.

"This hearing is convened to determine whether Programme Lament Archive constitutes unproductive sentiment within the meaning of the Efficiency Standards," Vell said, "and whether any subsequent allocation can be justified."

The door opened, and Whitmore came through with his walking frame, rubber feet whispering on the cord carpet. He wore a suit that fitted him like a secondhand opinion. Under one arm he carried the black leatherette folder, gold-stamped: LAMENT ARCHIVE — DOCUMENTATION.

He did not sit. He stood behind the respondent's table and leaned into the frame.

Vell read from the file: "Projected return on investment: absent. Completion status: achieved. Recommendation: records reclassified, no further allocation."

"There I must correct the record," Whitmore said. "I loaded the seeds myself. I loaded the soil myself. I sealed the handwritten pages in the vacuum canisters in my own hand. The satellite is in the orbit we wrote for it, out past Mars. It is the only thing this Ministry has ever filed that will still be moving when the Ministry's files have turned to dust. I call that a return. I call it the only return that matters."

"The completion of the project is not in dispute," Vell said. "What is in dispute is whether the allocation was justified within a relevant horizon."

"Relevant to whom? Your code stops at fifty years. After that there is nothing but blank paper. I sent the project to the blank paper. It is the only address worth writing to."

"Eight million years is not a horizon, Dr. Whitmore. It is the absence of one."

"It is the address of the future. We wrote to the thing this world will become when it is finished with itself. And because a vault is not complete without a person in it, we sent one girl's question along with the seeds." He looked at her. "You have the message in your file, Chief Examiner. Read it."

Vell turned a page. "The interim report quotes, in full, at footnote four: 'What the perfect mind calls waste / is the soil where the future blooms.' — A. Okafor, age seventeen."

"You read it aloud," Whitmore said. "Thank you. You have just closed your file and kept the page open."

"This is not a recital."

"On the contrary. You had to write my student's poem down in order to banish it. You printed it in the footnote. You quoted it in the report. Every file you close on it keeps it open. You could not have invented a more efficient preservation system if you had tried."

"The tribunal is not moved by irony."

"No, I don't suppose it ever has been." He shifted his weight, and for a moment she heard the strain in his arms. Then he was level again. "Let me speak plainly, then. The satellite contains seed, soil, and DNA from species your own ministry has recorded as declining. The vault is real, and the vault is in the dark, and the dark is one place your allocation code cannot reach. You may close the file. The vault does not open for files."

"The scientific payload is not in dispute."

"Then what is in dispute?" Whitmore asked. "A girl wrote two lines. You have built a tribunal to try two lines."

"We have built a tribunal to try the allocation of public resource to two lines."

"Sentiment," Whitmore said, tasting the word. "Every road in this city was built by sentiment. The hospital, the flood defence, the reason anyone wants a future to protect. Sentiment built the house this building sits in. You file it and call it efficiency, but the file is in the house sentiment built."

"The tribunal is not a debating society."

"No. It is a meeting about a poem. Somewhere the State has to meet the poem, and this is where it chose to meet." He gave Vell a long, exact look. "You are not burning the Lament. You cannot. It is past the red world. You are putting it in the ground."

The three heads bent together at the long table. The deliberation was quicker than Amara had hoped and slower than she needed. Then Vell turned back.

"The tribunal finds that Programme Lament Archive constitutes unproductive sentiment within the meaning of the Efficiency Standards. The project is disbanded. Records will be retained at the lowest retention tier. Telemetry acquisition is reclassified as residual and ceases. The tribunal thanks Dr. Whitmore for his service."

Whitmore stood a moment longer, gripping the frame. Then he set the black folder on the table and did not open it. "Thank you. I've had worse endings."

He came toward the observers. For a moment his eyes found Amara and held her—not sad, the other thing, the thing that was almost amused. Then the rubber feet carried him out, and the door closed like a file.

Dev Patel caught her in the corridor.

"You wrote the recommendation," she said.

"I wrote the file." He was still holding it. "I put the seed viabilities on page one. I put the soil modules on page two. I made them read the DNA assessment into the record. And they read it, and saw a poem, and that was the end."

"The poem was the payload, Dev. You were at the launch."

"I was at the launch. You cried, and I have never seen anything that real." He looked at his collar as though the horizon had appeared there without his consent. "But it can't insulate a house. It can't purify a river. It can't grow a crop before the thaw. It's beautiful, Amara. It isn't a return."

"It doesn't compete with the flood defence," she said. "It's the reason anyone wants a street to survive long enough to build a flood defence."

"You wrote two lines. There was a tribunal over two lines. That's attention spent on something that will not come back for—"

"Eight million years."

"Eight million years."

She said, "If it were finished, they'd have let it lie. But they couldn't let it lie. They had to come in person and close it in public. Whitmore says that's the most hopeful thing the Ministry has ever done."

"You believe that?"

"The alternative is that I'm the girl who wrote the waste."

Dev was quiet. At last he said, "It isn't waste. I put that in the recommendation, in the last paragraph, before my signature. They didn't take it out. They just didn't see it." He looked at her. "This was my first posting. I wanted you to know I tried."

"I know."

He walked to the lift with the file under his arm, and she let him go.

Whitmore was on the stone steps, sitting on a bench because the walk to the bus had become too long. She sat beside him. For a while neither spoke.

"They don't burn," he said. "They file. Fire is honest. Fire is a confession. Filing is how a civilisation tells itself it has kept everything while making sure nothing is ever found."

"It's in the ground."

"It is."

She helped him to the bus. Before boarding he looked at her. "I meant every word in there. That is the terrible thing. And I have never had a better hour."

On her desk that night, beside the cardboard Lament, lay the second letter she had drafted in the spring and never sent: *On the Measurable Returns of Wonder*. She added a postscript.

*Since drafting this, the Lament Archive has been disbanded by a tribunal of the Cultural Allocation Review. I ask that the seed manifest be preserved as a scientific document. A seed is not a sentiment.*

The reply came in three weeks, on grey paper. *Your submission has been received and filed.*

She wrote to Civic Efficiency. She wrote to the Office of Planetary Resources, requesting the seed manifest under the disclosure clauses. She wrote to Chief Examiner Vell herself: *Which of you will tell the next girl to write it down?* The replies were identical but for the reference number. *Received and filed.*

Then, in the public gazette, in the list of acquisitions ceased, she found the line she had been looking for:

*TELEMETRIC ACQUISITION, PROGRAMME LAMENT: CEASED. DATA: RETAINED, LOWEST TIER. CLASSIFICATION: RESIDUAL ATTACHMENT.*

*Residual attachment.* They had a word for the habit of caring. No one in any observatory would listen for the Lament now. Not because anyone was forbidden. Simply because there was nothing efficient to add. But the orbit was not a project. The orbit was a written sentence, and a written sentence goes on being a sentence whether or not anyone is there to read it aloud.

She bought a notebook with a stiff black cover, the kind meant for accounts, and on the first page wrote *Programme Lament — Working Ephemeris*. Under it she set down the orbital elements as Whitmore had given them: semimajor axis, eccentricity, inclination, longitude of the ascending node. The gold line translated into numbers. Each Sunday she advanced the calculation by her own hand. It was not a letter, not a poem. It was a row of figures that said, in the only language the Ministry could not file: *I am still attending.*

On a clear night in January she walked up through sleeping Greenwich Park to the observatory hill. The dome was dark. The gate still read SCHEDULED OBSERVING — AUTHORISED PERSONNEL & DEMONSTRATED OUTPUT ONLY. She did not try the gate. She stood in the cold above the city and said the couplet twice: first as the curse she had meant it to be, then as the key Whitmore had said it was. She no longer knew which reading was true. She no longer needed to. It had been read into the record of a tribunal. It had been printed in a footnote. It had been filed at the lowest retention tier. There was nowhere left for the Ministry to put it except the ground, and the ground was the thing that bloomed.

Somewhere beyond Mars the Lament carried the seeds and the soil and the voices and the one page that had become Exhibit A and outlived the exhibit. The orbit did not know the project had been disbanded, did not know its telemetry had been reclassified, did not need the Ministry's permission to go on being a written sentence.

The Ministry had closed the file.

The file had never been the thing she trusted.

She was twenty years old, and she had been planted.

chapters.name: Anti-Civic Sentiment
chapters.content:
## 8. Anti-Civic Sentiment

Spring was late that year. It arrived in grey gusts off the river, the kind of spring that never quite convinced anyone, and on a cold bright morning in early March the gate below the observatory was locked and a Ministry drone was already waiting over the path.

Amara helped Whitmore out of the taxi. He used the walking frame now the way other men used a briefcase, as something to carry and be carried by, and he stood for a moment getting his bearings, in the way he had once stood in front of classrooms, and then he nodded at the dark sheet under her arm.

“Put it up,” he said. “I’ll do the talking.”

She unfolded the trajectory plot. It was dark paper, a long thin gold line arcing across the solar system, the return arc a gold comma that had gone to the edge of the answer and decided to come back. It had hung above his gas fire in Catford for two years. This morning he had folded it himself into a shape his hands could manage; she had watched him take a long time about it, and had not offered to help.

Their audience was four people. Three university students who had been told the lecture was cancelled and had come to the hill on the rumour that it was moving, and a woman with a pram who stopped because two people holding a map of the solar system in the wind looked like something that might turn out to be interesting.

Whitmore cleared his throat. The drone lowered itself to six feet and blinked its red light.

“I had prepared a lesson,” he said. “It was going to be called ‘The Lament Archive: An Introduction.’ The University of Greenwich has determined that a lecture on the Lament no longer falls within its publicly demonstrated output horizon, so I have brought the lesson to the one place they cannot cancel. The pavement.”

He spoke quietly, exactly. Twelve years of teaching had taught him to make a lecture feel like a conversation. He told them about the drum of gold foil, the lead-lined seed modules, the soil from six continents, the six hundred human voices in languages that would die long before the capsule came back. He told them about the handwritten pages sealed under noble gas — cellulose, ink, hesitation. He told them what orbit did to a sentence. He did not raise his voice.

“The Ministry of Cultural Efficiency has classified the project as unproductive sentiment,” he said. “And I am to be recorded as something rather more active. Between us, I prefer it. I have been productive all my life. It is a relief to be recorded as the one thing I made that cannot be filed.”

He looked up at an angle, locating by memory the point beyond the yellow haze where the gold line was travelling. He raised his left hand to point, and the hand trembled, and fell back against the frame. He looked at it as if it had said something impertinent, and went on.

“The orbit is a sentence. It is finished, and it is still being written. The seeds are the words. The soil is the grammar. The page”—he nodded at the dark sheet in her arms—“is the gold line. Eight million years, and a comma at the end, coming back.”

The woman with the pram said, “That’s beautiful,” to no one in particular, and walked on. One of the students took out a phone and put it away, because there was no signal and no point. The drone recorded all of it.

They left the trajectory plot pinned to the gate with two drawing pins from his coat.

“Leave it,” he said, when she moved to take it down. “Let them photograph it until the rain takes it.”

On the walk back to the taxi, he said, as if continuing a sentence he had been carrying for years: “They don’t burn. They file. Fire is honest. Filing is how a civilisation tells itself it has kept everything while making sure nothing is ever found.” He stopped, pressed his lips together. “I’m repeating myself. That’s what a man does when he is running out of new things and wants to keep the old ones.”

A week later the notification arrived: a grey envelope, the levelled horizon line printed where a sender’s name ought to be. Whitmore asked her to read it aloud, not because his eyes had failed, but because holding a sheet steady, he said, “takes two hands, and I appear to be touring with a reduced company.”

She read:

“Notification of civil assessment. In respect of public remarks delivered on the fifth of March at the Royal Observatory gate, you are recorded as demonstrating anti-civic sentiment within the meaning of the Efficiency Standards. The recording has been retained at the lowest tier. Consequence: teaching licence revoked; all residual observatory access—including the reading room, the plateau, and the daylight clause—permanently withdrawn; any public assembly convened by you shall require prior written clearance.”

Three sentences. They had filed him almost as well as they had filed her poem.

“Residual observatory access,” Whitmore said. He seemed to be tasting it. “I was on the staff of this institution for twelve years, and my connection to the hill is now a residual attachment to an archival object. They have a word for everything except what they are doing.”

“What was the daylight clause?”

“On clear days I could sit in the reading room at the top of the hill and look at the river. I did it twice. You don’t need a telescope to attend.” He looked at the window and the grey air beyond it. “Now I attend from here. The view is worse. The arithmetic is the same.”

He pushed the pen across the table toward her.

“Sign the acknowledgment for me,” he said. “I can’t hold the thing.”

“If I sign it,” Amara said, “my name goes into the same file as yours. Your name is already in their footnote. I won’t put mine in the body.”

He looked at her for a long moment. “That’s my line. You’ve been sitting at my knee too long.”

“It’s my line now. I earned it.”

The pen had rolled to the edge of the table. Nobody moved to stop it. It dropped to the carpet, and lay there.

“There,” he said. “We have both declined to be filed.”

“They don’t need the acknowledgment.”

“No. They’ve already made it. Filing is the acknowledgment.” He looked at the pen on the floor. “The body is the cart. Mine has reached the end of the road. I staked everything on the words outlasting the cart.” He flexed his left hand and watched it, as if checking whether it had further objections. “It seems I won.”

She went to St. Jude’s in April. She did not fully know why. Some part of her believed the story of the launch could not be finished in the place where it had begun. She still had the cardboard Lament she had carried at Cornwall — silver foil, dish slightly lopsided, LAMENT with a full stop on its flank — and the folded newspaper photograph in her coat pocket. It seemed wrong for both of them to live in a drawer. She had also brought a sheet of paper with a heading she had written in blue ink: *Signatures requesting the reactivation of telemetric acquisition, Programme Lament*. No one had asked to sign it yet, but she had brought it.

Mr Osei came out to meet her before the first bell. He was smaller than she remembered, and his sentences arrived as if they had been formed elsewhere and delivered to him for safekeeping. “We’re not permitted to convene assemblies for non-curricular purposes, Amara. There’s a protocol. You’re welcome to stand at the gate. Many former pupils do.”

“At the gate,” she said.

“At the gate.” He looked at her kindly. “What happened to Dr Whitmore—several of the staff thought it was heavy-handed. But we teach the children to allocate their attention now. There’s a word for holding on to what cannot return. We have to teach the word too.”

He did not tell her the word. She did not ask.

The students came past her in a river. Some wore the levelled-horizon badge. Some carried grey folders printed HOPE: A BUDGET. The cardboard Lament received a few glances—it was shiny, and it was the kind of thing Year 8 made—and the glances moved on. The West Wall, where the newspaper article had been pinned for the whole shimmering weekend two years before, now held a display of allocation certificates.

The second bell. Most of the river had gone in. A girl stopped in front of the model, badge unpinned, held in her fist as if she had not decided whether it was going on.

“Is that the Lament? We did it in Efficiency module. Case study 3.2. You’re allowed to think it’s beautiful, but you have to classify it correctly.” She looked at Amara, at the photograph, back at the model. “You’re A. Okafor? The textbook says your poem proves its own point. It says it’s an example of unproductive sentiment, because it calls its own work waste.”

“No,” Amara said. “It says, what the perfect mind calls waste. The classification was theirs. It wasn’t the poem’s.”

The girl was quiet, looking at the lopsided dish. “That’s cleverer than the textbook says.”

“It’s not clever. It’s still flying.”

“Flying where?”

“Past Mars. Out past the Kuiper belt. The gravity turns it around, and in eight million years it comes back to the air above this hill.”

“That’s a long time. Who’s supposed to read it?”

“Whoever’s here. Maybe nobody. It doesn’t have to be read to be true.”

The girl looked at the badge in her hand, put it in her pocket, and went in through the doors without putting it on.

Amara found Mrs Abiola in the car park after school. She asked after the foil replica her Year 8 form had made for the launch, the one like a sunflower after rain.

Mrs Abiola looked at the ground. “During the materials-efficiency audit. It was beautiful, Amara. They weighed it.”

“They weighed it.”

“They weighed it, and the foil went to a recovery facility, and the card went to design, for core curriculum projects. The children made an allocation chart out of parts of it. I’m sorry. I should have hidden it.”

She opened her folder and took out a single torn corner of card. A curve of foil was still attached to it, crimped into the shape of the dish, the edge of the full stop. “I did hide this,” she said.

Amara took it. “It’s the dish. It’s the part that listened.”

At Greenwich, the launch was already a footnote in a footnote. The orbital mechanics syllabus had replaced its Programme Lament worked example with an asteroid resource assessment; her tutor had apologised to her once and never mentioned it again. The library’s copy of Whitmore’s textbook had been moved to closed stacks, which in the new language meant available, if you could demonstrate an output, which no one could.

On the way home she tried the municipal archive’s public terminal for the South London Press article. The search returned one line: RECORD RETAINED, LOWEST RETENTION TIER. Nothing else. The launch was not gone. It was stored, residual, and unreachable. Dismissal, not fire. The memory of the launch was not being burned. It was being put in a drawer so deep that the drawer became the forgetting.

She told Whitmore by going to Catford, because the telephone had become the one efficient thing they still shared, and she refused to file him in it.

He listened from his chair, hands in his lap like two things he had borrowed and was not sure he would return. The wall above the gas fire was empty. The pinpricks where the trajectory plot had hung made a faint constellation in the wallpaper.

She told him about the girl, the textbook, the weighed model. Then she set the torn curve of foil on the table.

He touched it with the back of his hand, the only part of him that still volunteered. “The dish,” he said. “That’s the part that listened.”

They were quiet for a while.

“They’ve made it official,” he said. “I can’t teach. I can’t observe. I can’t convene. They’ve weighed the model, filed the article, taught the next generation to file the launch. That’s the efficient version of erasing it. You don’t burn the thing. You teach the next generation to file it.” He looked at the curve of foil. “The girl will go home and think about the comma. That’s all a seed is—something a sentence leaves behind.”

“She put the badge in her pocket.”

“Good,” he said. “Good.”

She took out the black notebook and read him the week’s entry: the Lament’s hand-computed position, a point beyond Mars, each Sunday farther from the red world and farther from them. Her sums. Her attendance.

When she finished, he was looking at the empty wall. “The observatories have stopped listening,” he said. “You are the telemetry now.”

“I’m only doing the arithmetic.”

“The arithmetic is the attending.” He turned his head toward her. “They’ve filed the launch away, Amara. The launch is not in their files anymore. It’s in your notebook. That’s the only address it needs.”

She put the notebook back into her coat, over her heart, beside the grey report from the Ministry and the photograph that no archive would show her. The streetlight outside made a yellow haze of the air above the cars.

He said from the chair, “Are you still attending?”

“Every Sunday.”

“Then it’s not erased. It’s just not in their files.”

She walked home across the river under the wet spring streetlights, her hand in her coat on the notebook, the torn curve of foil in the other pocket, the gold line travelling on in the dark above her. They had silenced her mentor. They had taught the next generation to file the launch. But the orbit was a sentence, the sentence was in her care, and a sentence goes on being a sentence whether or not anyone is there to read it aloud.

chapters.name: Don't Let Them Teach You
chapters.content:
By the end of April the visits had become the geography of her week. Tuesday afternoons after orbital mechanics, Sundays after the arithmetic: two buses, the bench by the corner shop where she could watch for the 136, the stairwell with its smell of dust and boiled cabbage and the old woman's lavender. Whitmore left the door unlocked now, because the lock had become one more thing the cart could not manage, and she could hear the walking frame working the lino — step, shuffle, step — before she reached the top landing. She had begun to measure the distance between visits not in days but in the weakness of those sounds.

The emptiness of the wall was still the first thing she saw. The pinpricks remained, a faint constellation the drawing pins had left in the wallpaper — the ghost of the gold line that had hung above the gas fire for a year before going to the Observatory gate. Whitmore had found a better surface. “I’ve moved it up there,” he said the first time she caught him watching the ceiling. “Closer than the wall. Nothing to file.”

The ceiling was cracked plaster, yellowed by years of gas-fire heat, with a water stain in the far corner like a hasty map of an ocean. His eyes moved across it slowly, from the door to the window, following an arc she could not see. “It’s past the red world,” he said once, without looking at her. “Climbing toward the bending. You can see it if you don’t look.” She did not ask what he meant. She had learned that when he spoke of the orbit he was not always speaking of the satellite. The two ways of reading a thing — the curse and the key, the ground and the bloom — had merged in him, lately, into a single long attention, and the orbit was the only shape that attention could still travel along.

The reading was the one thing he could still ask for. At first he chose the books himself, naming shelf, row, spine while she stood on the step-ladder with her hand out. Then he stopped being able to name them. He would close his eyes and say, “Something about the long things. The slow ones,” and she learned to choose for him — the paperbacks with the cracked spines and the folded corners, scored in the margins by a younger hand. A 1963 *Practical Astronomy* whose chapter on the precession of the equinoxes claimed that the sky we point at is never the sky that will listen. His own doctoral thesis, typewritten and carbon-smudged, on the stability of long-period orbits: *Over sufficient time, every predicted path acquires a small and sacred doubt.* His eyes tracked the ceiling while she read, and when she stopped he said, “Leave it a moment. Let it hang there.” She learned to wait.

It was during one of those waits that she told him, again, about the girl at the gate — the badge unpinned in the fist, the textbook’s misreading, the question *who’s supposed to read it?* She had told him in April; she told him now because repetition was a form of holding, and because there were few things left to offer him. He said, “Good. Good,” the way he had said it the first time, and she saw that he had stored this one small germination against the dark the way the satellite stored the seeds.

While he slept the afternoons away, the Concord absorbed the last of the old institutions. The notices called it consolidation. The Royal Observatory, a place of listening for two hundred years and a museum for fifty, passed into the Ministry of Cultural Efficiency; the reading room was closed for “reprofiling,” and the telescopes were draped and the drapes photographed into the allocation record. The university followed within weeks; the astronomy collection, what remained of it, went from closed stacks to a building in Dagenham that Amara was not permitted to enter. She wrote to the Office of Planetary Resources for the seed manifest and received the answer she had memorised: *Your submission has been received and filed.* She wrote for Whitmore’s own file — forty years of work, the hearing, the loss of the daylight clause — and for the black leatherette folder he had left unopened on the tribunal table. The reply came in three lines: *RECORD RETAINED. RETENTION TIER: LOWEST. CLASSIFICATION: RESIDUAL.* It did not say which record. It never said which record.

She went once to the Observatory gate to see if the trajectory plot had survived the spring rain. It had not. The gate was bare, the drawing pins gone, and in their place a single grey notice. The ghost of the gold line had rejoined the ghost on Whitmore’s wall. At the municipal archive the public terminal returned the same one line for any search she attempted: RECORD RETAINED, LOWEST RETENTION TIER. It was the first time she understood in her body that dismissal was a kind of burial. They were not burning the thing. They were filing the thing, and the filed thing was as close to gone as a thing could be while still, technically, existing.

She did not tell him about her attempts. He knew anyway. “They’ve archived me before I’m dead,” he said, amused despite everything, and the laugh turned into the breathlessness that came more often now, and she held the glass of water while he drank, and the tracking went on above her head. “They’ll file the sky next. You watch. They’ll try to put a number on it. They can’t. A star is not a return. It’s a standing invitation.”

It was the last long sentence she ever heard him speak. The week the notice about the reading room appeared in the paper, he stopped getting out of bed. It was not a decision; the body was the cart, and the cart had refused the road. By the second week the flat had shrunk to one room — the bed by the window, the glass, the tin of pills, the bell she had bought at the chemist’s so he could call her from the kitchen. He never rang it. “I’m not a telescope,” he said when she pulled the curtains against the glare. “Don’t put the cap on me.” So she left the curtains open, and the June heat came through the glass like a hand, and with it the traffic of the South Circular, the ordinary moving world, so that the room contained both things at once: the static of daily life, and a man tracking the last slow arc of a line no one else could see.

The last time was a Thursday, or perhaps a Wednesday; by then the shape of the week had dissolved. She came in from the heat, past the lavender and the boiled cabbage, and found him with his hands folded on the sheet like a chart that had been closed. His eyes were on the ceiling. She sat in the chair and did not ask how he was, because the question had become its own kind of filing — a drawer you put the truth in — and instead opened the black notebook and read him the arithmetic. It was three days early, but the numbers had wanted to be written; she had worked them at the bus stop, in the green fug of the shelter, because the page had seemed to be waiting.

“It’s still there,” she said. “Still on the line. Past the red world, climbing toward the bending. The sentence in the canister, the aphelion in eight million years.”

He made a sound in his throat that might have been laughter.

She read to him then from the book with the cracked spine, the one she had taken from the shelf that morning because she had known — without letting herself know — that it would be the last. It was not a famous book. It was a book about the long things, the slow ones, written by a man who had never been efficient and never wanted to be. The passage was one he had marked; the corner of the page was folded into a small white wing.

“If you throw a stone into still water,” she read, “the wave that touches the far bank is not the stone. The stone is at rest at the bottom of the pond. What arrives is the pattern of its falling, translated into a new substance. The water does not know the stone; it knows only the shape of the leaving. And the far bank, when it is touched, cannot tell you where the stone has gone — only that something, once, was thrown.”

When she finished, the room held the passage for a moment, the way he had taught her to let a thing hang. Then she said, quietly, “They teach them the poem confesses its own waste. The ministry textbook. Case study 3.2. They quote the two lines to prove the whole Archive was nothing.”

His eyes had come down at last from the ceiling. They found her face, and she had the careful, absurd sense that he was reading her the way she had been reading the page — scanning for the shape of the leaving.

“Don’t let them teach you,” he said, “that a waste is never an investment.”

The sentence took the rest of what he had. He lay looking at her, checking that she had received it, and for a moment the tracking simply stopped. She understood that she was meant to answer him, and the answer came up out of her without being chosen — the old words, the blue-ink words, spoken into the room for the first time in his hearing since the night she had delivered them to his door:

*What the perfect mind calls waste*
*is the soil where the future blooms.*

His eyes held her face for a long moment. Then, as if something had been settled, they went back up to the ceiling, and the tracking began again — or perhaps it had never quite stopped. But the thread of it grew thin. She sat with the book open in her hands. Somewhere past Mars the Lament was climbing toward the bending, and on the South Circular a bus changed gear. At last the water stain in the corner of the ceiling was still, and the room took on a new quality — the quality of a sentence finished, now simply lying on the page.

She sat with him until the light changed. At some point she rang her mother from the landing, and Ngozi came on the bus in her hospice coat, and took over the practical world with a gentleness Amara had never seen pointed at anything but a patient. She closed the eyes, she made the calls, she opened the window a little wider, and she stood a moment in the kitchen with her hands flat on the counter, the position she took when the next thing could not be decided and had to be done anyway. Then she said, “Come home,” and Amara went.

The funeral was on the last grey day of a hot month, in the crematorium chapel off the South Circular. Whitmore had left instructions, in the way he had arranged everything at the end: cheapest cremation, no music, the library given to the charity shop or the weighing scales, whichever took it first. It was not a large gathering. Amara; her mother; Mrs Abiola, who had come from Lewisham and stood at the back, earning a place in the history of small acts; two retired men from the old Observatory who had not asked permission and were not sorry; the woman from the ground-floor flat, who had collected his post and would miss the walking frame. No one from the Ministry. They had filed him already. The chapel noticeboard, beside the order of services, carried a poster in the levelled-horizon grey: NOTHING SPENT ON NOTHING.

Amara did not speak. She had learned from him that you put the words in the cart and you push; the cart had reached the end of the road. She stood at the back with her hands in her coat pockets, the torn foil curve in one, the black notebook in the other, and at her chest, pressed over her heart, the newspaper photograph and the grey interim report.

Afterward, in the cold sun on the chapel steps, one of the old Observatory men shook her hand. “He used to say the sky was a library and I was a book he’d never finish. I never thanked him for it.” He looked at the flat grey sky, which was doing its best. “He said you were the one who read to him. He said that more than once.”

Mrs Abiola came to her last. “He was the one who told us the dish would listen,” she said. “I made the children make it crooked. Nothing that listens is perfectly straight, I said.” She pressed Amara’s hand, and it was warm, and it was done.

She did not go back to the flat when the landlord’s men came. She kept three things. The book with the cracked spine, which she took from the shelf the day after the funeral, because she could not bear for it to be weighed. The torn foil curve, still the dish, still the part that listened. And the sentence. On the night after the funeral she sat at the kitchen table in Lewisham with the black notebook open at the first page and wrote, in the same blue ballpoint: *Don’t let them teach you that a waste is never an investment. — EW* — and beneath it, where the orbital elements began, the next Sunday’s figures.

She carried the blank petition still, folded with the photograph and the grey report over her heart. Each Sunday she entered the Lament’s position — a little farther from the red world, a little nearer the great bending — because Whitmore had told her she was the telemetry, and the telemetry had to be somebody. It was not hope, exactly. It was not grief. It was the older thing: the decision to keep watching the place where a thing had been, because watching is a form of pointing, and pointing is a form of saying — *there. There it went. There it is.*

She was not willing to let the project go. She understood, now, that the project was not the rocket, or the gold foil drum, or even the page sealed in the canister. It was the pointing. It always had been.

Somewhere past Mars the Lament was climbing toward the bending. She was twenty years old, and she was still attending.

chapters.name: The Girl Who Would Not File Away
chapters.content:
# 10. The Girl Who Would Not File Away

Whitmore died in July. By the third Sunday in August, Amara had written the first letter.

It seemed, at the time, the only possible continuation of the arithmetic. The arithmetic was private; it lived in the black notebook and the Sabbath silence of the Lewisham kitchen. A letter was different. A letter was a hand extended toward a locked door. She wrote to the Ministry of Cultural Efficiency, care of the office that had disbanded the Lament Archive, and requested, under the disclosure provisions of the Cultural Allocation Review, access to the reclassified telemetric records of Programme Lament. She asked for the orbital elements as they stood since the cessation of acquisition. She asked whether retrieval had been scheduled. She asked who, if anyone, was listening.

The reply took six weeks. It was a single sheet of grey paper. *Your submission has been received and filed.*

Amara read it three times. Then she folded it along the crease and put it in the shoebox that had once held her mother's winter boots. There was a price in biro on the inside of the lid—*£34.99*, in Ngozi's patient hand, as if the purchase itself had needed to be filed. The shoebox already held three grey slips: the replies from Civic Efficiency, the Office of Planetary Resources, and Chief Examiner Vell, the ones she had gathered before Whitmore died. The new slip lay on top like something planted.

When she was nine, her father had made an eclipse out of a shoebox. She had kept that box for a whole year after he left, and her mother had thrown it out as just a box. Amara did not think about this when she put the grey slips into the new box. That would be a lie. She thought about it every time the lid went back on.

She wrote again in September. *Your submission has been received and filed.* She wrote in November to the Office of Planetary Resources, requesting the seed manifest under the disclosure clauses she had taught herself to cite from memory. *Your submission has been received and filed.* She wrote to the Deep-Space Division, to the Bureau of Scheduled Retrieval, to the office that might hold the black leatherette folder Whitmore had left unopened on the tribunal table. Every reply was the same efficient sentence, and Amara filed each one in its order, so that the shoebox became an archive of the word *no* spoken politely, grammatically, without a single wasted character.

In the back of the black notebook she kept a second ledger: LETTER ONE, LETTER TWO, LETTER THREE. By the time she turned twenty-one there were forty-three entries and the shoebox was half full. She did not think of it as despair. She thought of it as soil. The perfect mind would call it waste. She was learning to call it the ground under the future, and she kept writing because writing to a locked door was the only way she knew to keep her hand trained on the door.

---

The year she turned twenty-one, she graduated.

Her degree was no longer called Astronomy. The certificate read *Applied Celestial Mechanics*, with a module in resource trajectory analysis, and the cover carried the levelled horizon of the Concord, a line with nothing above it. Her mother wore her best coat and clapped, in the hall's hard acoustics, a half-second after everyone else. There was orange squash in plastic cups, and no one mentioned the poem. One of her lecturers, an old woman who had taught her perturbation theory out of a book whose spine had cracked open to the exact page of the Lament's long curve, shook her hand and said, very quietly, "The sky we point at is never the sky that will listen." Then she looked down at her collar, as though expecting a badge there, found none, and did not say another word. Amara thanked her by her first name. The woman nodded once, and was carried away by the crowd.

Amara worked the arithmetic that evening. On the Monday she went to the municipal records office, because the Concord's great work was filing, and filing required hands.

She typed classifications all day. ACTIVE, RETENTION, RESTRICTED, and the deepest category, the one that sank below the reach of any schedule: LOWEST TIER. The words drained of colour within a month; they were only shapes, only keys. She processed the files of dead projects and living citizens with the same even pressure, and her supervisor praised her steadiness. On her lunch breaks she used the staff terminal to request the Lament's telemetry logs. The system replied: *RECORDS MOVED TO DEEP-STORE. RETRIEVAL ON REQUEST.* She requested. *RETRIEVAL NOT SCHEDULED.* She requested again, with the citation number, and again. The answer never changed, because the answer had been written once, in a single efficient sentence, and no one had ever scheduled it to be reread.

One afternoon a file crossed her desk in error. A citizen's correspondence profile. Her own name, in a column she was not supposed to see, and in the classification field two words she knew better than her own date of birth: *RESIDUAL ATTACHMENT.* The file was not angry. It did not accuse. It expressed, with perfect administrative calm, the terms on which she would be permitted to go on existing. She closed the file. She did not print it. She went home and wrote the fifty-first letter.

---

The winter she turned twenty-three, she took a day of annual leave and went to Dagenham.

The astronomy collection had been moved there three years earlier, to a building she could not enter; she had the address from a freight manifest filed under *PUBLICLY DEMONSTRATED OUTPUT HORIZON*, which she suspected had been placed there precisely so that no one would find it. The building sat behind a wire fence at the end of an industrial road: windowless, long, with a loading dock and a single grey door. Amara stood across the street for an hour with the torn foil curve in her pocket, pressing her thumb against the crimped edge. *The dish. The part that listened.* Nothing entered or left. A van coughed at the gate and was waved through; the building absorbed it without acknowledgment.

She stayed until the vigil began to look, to any observer, like loitering. Then she walked to the bus stop and wrote the fifty-second letter on her knee, on the back of a grey slip she had brought for paper, because the office had stopped issuing her new forms, and because she was learning that the world gave you its refusals and expected you to make something of them.

---

The spring she turned twenty-five, a grey slip came through the letterbox. *CITIZEN CONTRIBUTION ASSESSMENT.* Date, time, room, and the instruction to bring proof of contribution. The letter was briefer than her refusals. It was, she thought, the first piece of correspondence from the Ministry to reach her without the word *filed* in it, and that was somehow worse.

She almost put it in the shoebox and stayed home. But five years of Sunday arithmetic had taught her something about attendance: you went, even when you knew the gate would refuse you, because attendance was a form of evidence. She went on the Tuesday, through a low building near the river, along a corridor of green-grey lino, to Room 17. She opened the door.

Dev Patel sat behind the table.

---

He was no longer the boy in the orange jacket. The uniform had a silver bar on the collar and a small levelled horizon over the left breast. He was reading a file that bore her name, and when he looked up his face passed through surprise into something else—relief, perhaps, or grief, or the memory of a clifftop at dawn, shared a long time ago by two people who had not been children even then.

"Amara."

"Dev."

He reached for the jug of water, poured a glass, and did not drink it. A blue ink stain rode the side of her hand, as it had when she was seventeen. He looked at it and did not say anything. Then he gestured to the chair, and she sat, and the assessment began.

The questions were soft-handed and inevitable. Employment. Output. Training. Plans. She answered. He typed. The river beyond the reinforced window ran grey in the rain. When the questions ran out, he sat back, his hands flat on the table on either side of the terminal, the way her mother's hands lay flat on a counter when the next thing had to be done and could not yet be decided.

"You're still writing the letters," he said.

"Yes."

"You're still doing the arithmetic."

"Every Sunday."

He nodded, as though he had known and had not wanted to know. "I heard about Dr. Whitmore." A pause. "I would have come."

"No one from the Ministry came," Amara said. "They had filed him already."

"I didn't mean—" He stopped. The sentence did not recover. He looked at the river for a moment and then said, "The project was beautiful, Amara. It was the most beautiful thing I have ever seen do nothing. I stood on a cliff and watched a girl cry over a cardboard satellite, and I have never forgotten it. But beauty without return is still without return. We can't afford nothing anymore." He said it as though it were a law of nature and not a choice. "That's the whole doctrine and the whole cruelty of the time we're in. My mother is alive because a machine was moved out of another ward and into hers. I stood beside her bed and watched her breathe, and I thought: the Lament did nothing for this. It was beautiful. It was nothing."

Amara took the folded petition from her coat and laid it on the table between them. Five years of pocket heat had softened the paper until it lay like a leaf.

"I've been carrying this since I was twenty," she said. "It asks for the reactivation of telemetric acquisition for Programme Lament. No one has signed it."

Dev looked at it. He did not touch it. "That's not a return."

"No."

"Amara. The river is rising."

"The river has always been rising." She had rehearsed this in the kitchen; she had said it to the shoebox; she said it now without rancour, as a fact. "The Lament was never meant to stop the river. It was meant to make sure that when the water goes down there is still a reason to build the next thing. The machine that saved your mother exists because someone, somewhere, decided a ward full of dying people was worth a machine. That decision is not arithmetic. It is a sentence someone wrote before the machine was built. The Lament is the same kind of sentence. It doesn't dialyse anyone. It doesn't hold back the flood. It says the future is worth writing to. You only build a river wall if you believe there is a future, Dev. Somebody has to be the one who writes to it first. Whitmore was the one. I'm the one now. When the next girl comes, she'll be the one."

"The textbook says the poem calls its own work waste."

"It doesn't. *What the perfect mind calls waste.* The classification was theirs. It was never the poem's. The poem was the answer."

Dev set his hands flat again. "You're not going to file it away."

"No."

He closed his eyes. When he opened them they were bright with the grey light off the river. "Five years ago I wrote the recommendation on that project. I wrote, in the last paragraph, before my signature: *It isn't waste.* They never read it. They read the poem and filed the recommendation with the project." He tapped the terminal. "There is a note on every letter you've sent. *Citizen known. Correspondence reviewed. No action required.* I've been the one writing it. I've been the watchman, Amara. I made sure no one decided you were worth stopping. After this month I can't do it anymore. They're transferring me to the regional allocation board. The office that receives your letters will be automated. The machines don't know your name. They'll triage you into the lowest engagement tier. They'll stop answering, because the machine will have decided you are not retrievable."

Amara heard the word before he spoke it. "Obsolete."

"Yes." He said it gently, the way you set down a sheet of glass. "They've already tagged your profile for it. The clerks have a name for you, too. It travels through the offices like a joke, or a small marvel. *The girl who would not file away.* A citizen whose file won't close because she keeps writing to the file. They don't say it kindly. They don't say it cruelly. They say it as a classification."

"The girl who would not file away." The phrase sat in the green-grey room like a stone in a pond. She thought of the cracked-spine book, the stone and the falling, the pattern that touched the far bank long after the throwing hand had gone. "That's not a joke, Dev. That's the whole of it. They file the thing. I refuse. The refusal is the wave. It doesn't matter whether they read it. It's still travelling."

"You can't feed a city on a wave."

"Maybe not. But you can't build one without it either."

At the door, she turned. "My mother is alive because of the machine in the other ward. I know what the Concord has paid for, and I don't deny it.
