But I am alive because you wrote *It isn't waste* and meant it, even in secret. You told me, and I have carried it the way I carry the orbit. That's not nothing. That's a seed."

His eyes were bright. He did not let them spill. "Be careful, Amara."

"I'm not going to stop."

"I know."

---

The notice came two weeks later, after the transfer, from an automated address she did not recognise. Grey paper, like all the others. She read it standing at the kitchen counter while the strip light stuttered and the kettle's breath fogged the window.

*CITIZEN NOTICE. Classification: obsolete. Rationale: unproductive persistence in respect of a closed record; sustained non-conversion of civic attention into measurable output. Effect: correspondence will not be acknowledged; community services will be graded at the lowest tier; retrieval of the citizen's file from active planning is not scheduled.*

She read it twice. Then she folded it along the crease and took down the shoebox. It was full; she had to press the lid for the new paper to fit. The lid accepted it. The box closed. The word *obsolete* lay at the top of the stack, above forty-odd refusals and a price in biro that nobody would ever claim.

Ngozi came in from a shift. She saw the shoebox on the table, the grey paper, and her daughter's face. She did not ask. She put the kettle on, and when the tea was poured she said, "What word did they use?"

"Obsolete."

Ngozi nodded. She touched the breast pocket of her hospice coat, where the newspaper clipping had lived for eight years, over her heart. "They have a word for the ones who won't stop holding a hand through the night. The form has a column now. Projected recovery classified as *waste.* I leave it blank." She turned, and her face was not angry. It was older, tired, and sure. "They file the living and the dead and the words they cannot use. But they cannot file what they cannot name. The clipping is still there. It has been over my heart for eight years." She tapped the pocket. "It's still going."

Amara looked at the shoebox, the grey lid, the word inside it. "It's still going," she said, and meant the Lament, and meant her mother's paper heart, and meant herself.

---

On the first Sunday after the notice, she did the arithmetic at the kitchen table.

The black notebook lay open under the lamp. At the top of the first page, in blue ballpoint: *Don't let them teach you that a waste is never an investment. — EW.* Below it, the orbital elements she had copied from the dark paper Whitmore had pinned above his fire: semimajor axis, eccentricity, inclination, longitude of the ascending node. Below those, in her own hand, the slow accumulation of Sundays—the sentence of the orbit advancing past the red world, climbing toward the bending, the same two ways of being read, curse and key, ground and bloom.

She worked the figures slowly, the way he had taught her, the way the long things had to be read. The torn foil curve lay beside the notebook. The cardboard Lament stood on the shelf behind her, its silver gone dusty, its wonky dish still crimped with the full stop. Outside, the city ran on the levelled horizon; the offices were filing her at the lowest tier; the machines were deciding not to retrieve her.

When the arithmetic was done, she wrote at the bottom of the page, in the same blue ballpoint, two words. *Still attending.* Then she closed the notebook and placed it inside her coat, over her heart, beside the folded petition and the photograph the archive no longer scheduled to retrieve.

They had called her waste. They had put her in the lowest tier, where nothing was scheduled to be found. But a filed thing is not a burned thing. The girl who would not file away had been filed at last, and the file was retained, and the file went on existing in the dark. Somewhere beyond the red world, the gold line climbed, and the sentence was still being written, and the telemetry was still attending. The ground did not keep accounts. The ground was the thing that bloomed.

chapters.name: The Records Are Not Burned
chapters.content:
The directive arrived on a Tuesday, in a grey envelope with a grey line printed across the flap, addressed to all classification staff. Amara opened it with the communal letter opener and read the title twice before she understood it: *Archival Deprioritization Protocol — A Guide to the Continued Retention of Scheduled Records.* The paper had the quality of all Concord paper now, heavy enough to be kept, thin enough to be nothing.

Mrs. Ellery read it to the room anyway, because Mrs. Ellery read everything aloud.

She stood at the front of the open-plan office with her cardigan buttoned to her throat and the memo held at arm's length. The fluorescent tube above her hummed its one cautious note. Outside, the river threw grey light at the window, and the light died against the glass. "As of this cycle," she announced, "all records currently held at the lowest retention tier shall be re-coded under the heading of *residual emotional attachment to archival objects*. This is not a change of status. The records are retained. The records are complete." She looked up at them, pleased with the shape of the sentence, and repeated it so they would hold it. "Ongoing access derives not from operational need but from attachment to the objects themselves. What you feel for a record — that is what the record is classified under. Not the record's value. Your feeling."

Ruth in the next bay said, "So nothing gets thrown out." She said it the way people said amen.

Mrs. Ellery smiled. "Nothing gets thrown out. We are not barbarians. We keep everything. We keep it forever." She folded the memo and tapped it against her wrist like a little ruler. "A reshuffle, then. Not a purge. Home by five."

Amara's fingers rested on the keyboard, very still. She had heard Whitmore's voice in three sentences of Mrs. Ellery's speech — *kept, complete, not burned* — and she had heard the difference underneath, the way she heard the second line of the couplet underneath the first. Fire was honest. Fire confessed. Filing said *we have kept everything*, and the keeping was the grave. The new heading made the wanting the crime and the wanted thing only the evidence. They had found a way to file her heart in the same cabinet as the thing her heart was attached to.

The stamps arrived mid-morning, in a flat grey box with a grey foam bed, as though the old stamps had been eggs. The new one said RESIDUAL EMOTIONAL ATTACHMENT, the words crammed together to fit the width of the handle, so that EMOTIONAL leaned against RESIDUAL as if trying to get out from under the weight. Mrs. Ellery pressed it onto an old school record to demonstrate, turned the page so the room could admire the impression, and left the batch on Amara's desk. "You're steady," she said, as she always did. "Work down the lists."

Amara stamped the first file. It was the South London Press page, photographed and filed before the paper's archive had been folded into the municipal records: LEWISHAM STUDENT'S POEM SET FOR EIGHT-MILLION-YEAR VOYAGE. She read the headline, then the couplet, in grey flagstaff type that had never touched real paper, because the page itself had gone to scrap long ago and only its photograph remained. She stamped her own poem *residual emotional attachment*, set the file in the box, and thought of standing on the hill at Cornwall while the rocket climbed into the dawn. The file held the shape of the event. The event itself had already gone.

She worked down the list, open, stamp, close, stack. A national poetry curriculum: *residual*. A database of endangered dialects, each entry a set of words no one would speak in a hundred years: *residual*. And then a filmed demonstration recorded on a pavement outside the Royal Observatory gate, a man at the gate, a woman with a pram, three students, a long gold line pinned to the bars with drawing pins. She stamped it, and the stamp went through her like a pulse. The file jacket was grey, but the photograph inside it had been taken in colour, and the man's face was turned up to the daylight of an early March morning, speaking to no one who was required to listen. RECORD RETAINED, the jacket said. RETENTION TIER: LOWEST. And now the new heading, overprinting the whole body of it, pressed there by the weight of her own wrist. She had stamped the word down on Whitmore. That was what the job was.

The trolley came at lunchtime, when the office was half-empty and the kettle had boiled and failed. Grey boxes on grey shelves, the new words already on the lids, a printed list of series to be re-coded. She worked down the list with a ruler, half a second per line, until the ruler stopped.

PROGRAMME LAMENT (ARCHIVE HISTORY).

She looked at the line until the line began to look back. She had typed that name into a hundred request forms over five years; she had never seen it written down as a closed series, given a shelf-place among all the other closed things. She pulled the series card from the cabinet. A grey card, thin as a biscuit, with the old retention line scored out and the new paragraph beneath in fresh grey ink that still had its shine:

*The historical record of the above-named programme is held to be of no operational value. Continued retention is required for legal completeness. Requests for retrieval are presumed to derive from residual emotional attachment to the archival objects of the programme. Such requests are not actionable. Requests will be filed with the record.*

She read it slowly, the way Whitmore had taught her to read, holding each sentence in the air until it was done. *Residual attachment to the archival objects of the programme.* Her fifty-two letters were not answers to the record; they were symptoms of attachment to the record. The whole history of the Lament — the seeds, the soil, the six hundred human voices, the two lines in blue ink sealed under noble gas — had been folded into her feeling about it. They had not burned a single page. They had reclassified the page as a feeling, and the feeling as a filing problem, and the filing problem as solved.

She turned the card. CONTENTS, on the back, in a careful grey hand that had not needed to write for years now: *Canister one: seed modules (surrogate). Canister two: soil samples (surrogate). Canister three: cellulose page (digital surrogate retained at lowest tier).* Copies of copies. The real things were beyond the red world, still climbing, and the Ministry held the shadows. Even the digital surrogate of her own page — two lines scanned, greyed, compressed into the tier where nothing was scheduled — required a request, and every request required a feeling, and every feeling was a classification.

She tested it anyway. At the staff terminal, in the hush after lunch, she typed the request with the same care she gave the Sunday arithmetic — the Lament's name, the post-cessation telemetry, the disclosure clause. The machine answered at once, which was new. There used to be a pause, a small space as though a clerk were reading. Now the grey letters assembled themselves without any pause at all.

RETRIEVAL REQUEST — STATUS: NOT ACTIONABLE. REQUEST RE-CLASSIFIED AS RESIDUAL EMOTIONAL ATTACHMENT. REQUEST FILED WITH THE RECORD.

She read it twice, and then a third time, and on the third reading she understood the whole architecture. Her wanting had been entered into the file that could not be opened without wanting it. They had built a door so that the knocking became part of the wall.

A young man came to the public desk at half past two. He was seventeen, maybe, in a school coat missing a button, and he asked in a voice that tried not to shake whether there was anything left of the Lament Archive. Amara watched the clerk — a girl she did not know, newly appointed, steady — read the card by rote. "The records are retained," the clerk said. "Retained in full. They're just not scheduled for retrieval."

"What does that mean?"

"It means they're kept."

"But I can't see them?"

"I'm afraid not."

"It's supposed to be complete," the young man said. "Complete means it's all there. How is it complete if nobody can look at it?" The clerk had no answer. Amara had an answer, but she was not the clerk. The young man waited a moment, then left, and the door took him. Through the window she watched him stand on the pavement, do up his coat against the wind, and walk away down the embankment with the whole weight of her own hopelessness in his shoulders. She thought of Whitmore's last sentence — *a waste is never an investment* — and wondered what he would have said to the boy. *Write it down anyway,* he would have said. The boy did not know that yet. He would be taught to call it attachment, and then to call it residual, and then to stop coming to the desk at all, and the records would remain complete.

At tea break she took the photograph from the inside pocket of her coat.

She knew her own face without studying it — seventeen, Cornwall, the cardboard Lament held up like an offering, the foil dish catching the dawn. The photographer had asked her to look like she was looking at something beautiful, and she had obliged because it was true. What she needed was the other face in the frame. Whitmore stood half a step behind, leaning on his cane, caught by the shutter at the instant before the rocket left the pad: a man watching the future depart and being glad of it. The paper had gone soft along the folds, nearly thin as cloth after eight years over her heart.

If the Ministry knew this square of paper existed, it would be an archival object. Her keeping it would be attachment to an object. They would call her heart a classification and file the classification with the record, and the record would be complete, and the completeness would be the grave. That was the cruelty of dismissal. It did not burn. It renamed. It took everything a life had spent eight years learning to say and gave it a filing code, so that anyone reading the code would read nothing at all. Fire left a gap you could grieve. Filing left a record that was complete, and the completion was the grave — the photographs in jackets, the jackets in boxes, the boxes in the deep store, and over all of it the small grey stamp that said the only feeling the record could produce in a citizen was the feeling of having wanted her own past back. She folded the photograph and returned it to her pocket. They did not know about the photograph. She had learned to be enough.

The last file of the day was an old one. She knew it before she saw the name, by the crease at the top corner where it had been handled and returned a dozen times over the years. *WHITMORE, ELIAS. RECORD RETAINED. RETENTION TIER: LOWEST.* And beneath the old line, the new heading waiting: *CLASSIFICATION: RESIDUAL EMOTIONAL ATTACHMENT.* She understood in her body what she had known in her head at the tribunal: the reply that had never said which record it meant had found its body at last. Whitmore, filed. Not burned. Buried in a grey card in a grey cabinet, in the grey dark of a well-kept account, beside the surrogates and the closed histories and the fifty-two letters of the girl who would not stop asking.

Mrs. Ellery came by at five past five and said, "You've done well today. No one's been through so much as you." She meant the volume.

Amara set the stamp down. The records were not burned. The records were kept, preserved, complete. Her asking was in the file, but the asking was not all of her. She buttoned her coat over the photograph and walked home through the yellow dark, and the word came up in her the way the ground came up in the spring. *Residual.* What remained after the useful part had been taken away. They thought it was an insult. But she had spent eight years learning what the ground does with what remains: it takes it in. It keeps it. It does not keep accounts. She had known that truth as a curse once, and then as a key, and now it was simply the soil under everything else. They had filed her heart with the record, but the heart was still in her coat, still climbing, still the telemetry of a thing they had scheduled to be lost.

At home, under the lamp, she opened the black notebook at the head where Whitmore's sentence stood in blue ballpoint, and she worked the Sunday arithmetic three days early because the dark outside the window required it. The gold line advanced past the red world, climbing toward the bending. Somewhere beyond the reach of any request, in canister three, under noble gas, the two lines of blue ink were still the last page on top. And at the bottom of her own page, in the same blue ballpoint, she wrote the two words she had been writing for five years:

*Still attending.*

She closed the notebook, placed it inside her coat, over the photograph, over her heart, and let the sentence of the orbit carry on being written in the dark. The records were not burned. The girl was not filed. The wanting was not residual — the wanting was the part that listened, and the part that listened was still going.

chapters.name: The Rally
chapters.content:
The posters went up in the third week of May, over the hoardings and the bus shelters, across the sticker-scarred glass of the phone kiosks, in the windows of shops that had paid their cultural allocation. THE CONCORD INVITES YOU. TRAFALGAR SQUARE. THE SHAPE OF EFFICIENCY. COME AND SEE THE HORIZON HELD LEVEL. The levelled line ran gold across the bottom of every sheet, and beneath it, smaller, the slogan that had moved off the paper and into the mouths of the city: NOTHING SPENT ON NOTHING.

Amara saw the first one on her way to the records office, pasted over the window where the florist's used to be, and she stood in front of it until the woman at the bus stop looked at her twice. She did not think, I will go. The thought was already in her, planted, and the poster was only the weather that let it come up. She went because she was obsolete. There was no plan into which she now fitted, no queue she could join or jump; the city had scheduled her not to be going anywhere at all. It was a terrible freedom, and it was the only freedom she had.

She made the sign on Friday night at the kitchen table. The cardboard came from the box that had held tinned soup, the back of it smooth and brown, and she cut it down with kitchen scissors until it was a rectangle she could carry. The paint was a tin of black poster paint left over from something, nobody remembered what, and the brush had gone stiff and she worked it soft again in the sink. She painted the letters slowly, in the same careful way she worked the Sunday arithmetic, and she let her hand shake, because nothing that listens is perfectly straight.

WHAT THE PERFECT MIND CALLS WASTE.

She painted WASTE larger than the rest, at the end, where the eye would arrive and stop. When the paint was dry she sat back and read it twice, once as a curse and once as a key, then propped it against the wall. She thought about adding the second line—she even unstoppered the paint again, ready. But the second line was the answer, and she was not going to Trafalgar Square to answer them. She was going to show them their own word before they could use it on the next girl. Let the sentence stay open. Let it be the door.

She left the house at ten on Saturday, the sign wrapped in a plastic bag under her arm like something she was carrying to the dump. The morning was bright and hard, the kind of light that made the levelled-horizon posters look newly gilded. The pavements were full of people moving in the same direction, families with children on shoulders, old men with folding stools, a boy in an Administrative Corps training shirt singing the anthem under his breath. Nobody looked at her. That was the gift of being obsolete: even with a rectangular thing under her arm, she was the most unremarkable person on the street. She had spent her life learning to be invisible. Now the city confirmed it free of charge.

Trafalgar Square was already full when she arrived. The stage had been built at the foot of the column, a flat grey platform draped with the levelled horizon, and above it the National Gallery carried a banner so wide it seemed to hold the whole building down: EIGHT MILLION HOURS OF EFFICIENCY. She did not do the arithmetic. The loudspeakers were playing something smooth and percussive, and the crowd moved against the barriers like a single slow animal, patient, fed, sure of itself. She stood at the back for a while, watching the drones hang in the air like fat black bees, and then she unwrapped the sign.

She had expected a moment of exposure, a turning of heads, a steward's hand on her arm. What happened was quieter. The people nearest her read the sign and their faces changed in small ways—a tightening, a blankness, a careful looking away—and a little space opened around her, the way water opens around a stick dropped into it. A man in a grey tabard appeared at the edge of that space and looked at the sign, then at her face, then at the sign again, as though the two things did not quite fit together.

"You'll want to come with me," he said.

"Am I being arrested?"

He laughed: a real, small laugh, almost kind. "Nobody gets arrested at these. It's a data study. They can't study you in the middle of all this—you'd be crowd data, you'd be noise. Perimeter's cleaner for everyone."

He did not take her arm. He walked beside her, one hand lifted slightly, steering her with his body the way you might steer a shopper away from an open trapdoor, and the crowd parted for them without resentment. She carried the sign at her side, and nobody tried to take it from her. That was the thing she would remember later, more than the speeches: that nothing was seized, nothing was torn, nothing was burned. She was simply moved, gently, to where she could be seen properly.

The perimeter was a line of metal barriers at the edge of the square, behind which stood the people the rally had no use for: a woman with a pram and a sleeping child, an old man with a folded stool, two students sharing one set of headphones, a man in a stained coat talking to himself in a low, patient voice. The marshal placed her behind the barrier as if he were placing a glass on a shelf. "Stay here and you'll be fine," he said. "They'll have you on the system, but it's just the system. Nobody's going to do anything."

"Who's 'they'?"

He nodded toward the edge of the square, where a grey van sat with a bank of lenses on a mast and a dish that turned slowly, catching the light. CIVIC DATA—BEHAVIOURAL ANALYSIS UNIT, in letters so small you had to be standing beside it to read them. A woman sat at a fold-out table with a screen that showed the square cut into green sectors, each head a dot, each dot trailed by a line of numbers. Amara looked at the screen for a long moment and understood, without being able to say how, that one of the dots was hers.

"That's it?" she said.

"That's it." The marshal was already turning away. "You don't get a story out of it. You get a study."

He went back to the crowd, and the crowd closed behind him, and Amara stood behind the barrier at the edge of the square with her sign, among the pram and the folded stool and the man talking to himself, and watched the rally go on without her.

The loudspeakers swelled. A woman's voice came over them, amplified until it seemed to come from the sky itself: "Hope is a budget. Spend it where it grows." The crowd roared the last four words back at her, and the roar rolled off the buildings and came back smaller, like a wave returning. Amara had heard the voice before, in the Greenwich refectory, on the radio, in the mouths of her colleagues repeating it as a joke and then, gradually, no longer as a joke. Praetor Lenore Voss was speaking now, and the square was a single held breath. "For a generation we were told that nothing could be thrown away, that every hope deserved a chance, that the future would forgive us anything. The future does not forgive. The future is a budget, and we have balanced it. We have spent nothing on nothing. We have ended the Long Crises because we learned to stop pouring the river into the sand."

The crowd roared again. From the perimeter it sounded like weather, like something that would happen whether or not anyone was there to hear it. Amara looked at her sign. The black letters were dry now, flaking slightly at the edges where the brush had caught. WHAT THE PERFECT MIND CALLS WASTE. The sentence sat in her hands, unfinished, and the unfinishedness was the whole point. Let it be the door.

A small boy had worked his way to the barrier beside her, holding a strip of something that might once have been a flag. He read the sign aloud, sounding it out in a high, clear voice: "What, the, per—perfect—mind—calls—waste." His mother reached down and pulled him back by the shoulder, smiling the tight smile of a woman who did not want a conversation with the perimeter people. The boy looked at Amara over his shoulder, not at her face but at the sign, as though it were a thing he had been told not to touch and was touching anyway with his eyes.

"Bit of a long message, love," said the woman with the pram, without rancour.

"It's from a poem."

The woman considered this. "Well, it's a nice bit of painting." She rocked the pram; the child slept on. "My daughter would've been about you. She says there's no point to anything now. I tell her the point is you're alive." She did not ask what the poem was. Perhaps she did not want to know. Perhaps she knew already.

The rally continued. Voss's voice rose and fell; the crowd chanted, "Spend it where it grows," until the words lost their shape and became just sound, a heartbeat with a mouth. Twice Amara saw the crowd part and caught a glimpse of a silver collar bar, a levelled horizon over a breast pocket, a profile she knew. The first time she thought she was wrong. The second time the figure turned—and it was him, it was Dev, older, the same face under the same disciplined stillness—and he raised four fingers at her, the way he had done in Room 14, and put his hand where it could not be seen, and the crowd closed over him. She did not know what four fingers meant. She had never known. It was enough that he had seen her and had not looked away.

The speech ended. The anthem played, one long sustained note that filled the square and then emptied it, the way a held breath empties a room. The crowd began to disperse, streaming past the barrier in rivulets, and the drones drifted up and away like thoughts being dismissed. Amara stayed where she was until the square was nearly empty, until the grey van had folded its mast and driven off and the man with the folded stool had gathered up his stool and gone. The woman with the pram nodded to her as she left. The small boy had been carried away long before, his flag trailing.

She walked home through the yellow evening with the sign under her arm, unwrapped now, the black letters facing the street as if they were still on display. No one stopped her. No one asked. She had gone to the centre of the city and stood at its edge and held up a sentence, and the city had absorbed her and recorded her and let her go, and it had not once touched her, and that was the terrible thing. Fire was honest. Fire was a confession. Filing was how a civilisation told itself it had kept everything while making sure nothing was ever found. And there had been no fire. There had been a van with a dish, and a woman at a screen, and a green dot that was her, trailed by a line of numbers that would be read by no one and deleted by no one, because the Concord did not delete. The Concord kept. It kept everything. It kept it forever.

At home she propped the sign against the wall beside the dusty cardboard Lament, where the two of them stood like witnesses to different versions of the same act. She made tea. She opened the black notebook at the head where Whitmore's sentence stood in blue ballpoint, and she worked the arithmetic because the dark outside the window required it, and she wrote at the foot of the page, in the same blue ballpoint, three words: Still attending.

She did not know that the van had kept her face. She did not know that the face would be stored in a building whose address she would never be given, in a file whose number no one would ever speak aloud, under a classification that had not yet been invented for it. She thought she had been filed, and filed she was. But the Concord's method had always been the keeping. They could not burn her. They could only keep her. And what they kept could not be unkept. The footage would lie there in the dark, a small square of a woman holding up the first line of a poem on a May afternoon, waiting for the day when something—a fault, a question, a glitch in the great humming order—would open the file and find, not a specimen, but a girl who had refused to be finished.

It would outlive her. It would outlive the Concord. That was the gift and the crime, both at once. She had not known, standing behind the barrier, that she had been planted.

She drank her tea. The sign leaned against the wall. The notebook lay closed inside her coat, over the photograph, over her heart, and the words at the foot of the page were still going.

chapters.name: The Librarian
chapters.content:
In the year after she carried the sign to Trafalgar Square, the records office got a stamping machine before it got a new name. The machine was grey, the same grey as the refusals, and it could stamp RESIDUAL EMOTIONAL ATTACHMENT faster than she could and more evenly, and it never had to stop and rub its wrist. Mrs. Ellery stood beside it for three mornings, watching it work, and on the fourth she said, "You're steady," as if to the machine, and retired.

Amara did not grieve the office. She had learned to type there, which was useful, and she had learned to read classifications without reading the documents, which was not. When the manager asked where she should be reallocated, she said the library. The Concord allowed libraries to exist quietly. They were not worth the trouble of closing; nobody claimed they produced the future, but they cost almost nothing, and a library the state simply left alone would eventually finish with itself.

The Lewisham library was a grey building with a faded mural of a river that no longer had a name. Its catalogue had been digitised, then de-prioritised, then half-forgotten. The terminals still worked; the records they returned were marked NOT IN ACTIVE CATALOGUE, which meant that the book was present in the building and absent from the world. Amara's official duties were to receive returns and shelve them where the system would not look again. But she gave herself a quieter duty too: when a book was withdrawn from the catalogue and the collection van failed to come — the van always failed to come — she shelved it anyway, in a bay the plan never visited, where the dust lay so old it had a texture. A book no longer catalogued was not the same as a book no longer present. Whitmore had taught her that, and she had spent her twenties confirming it, mostly alone.

On Sundays she advanced the Lament's orbit by hand. The figures had climbed past the first bend at Mars years ago; the pencilled curve on the wall of her flat, copied from the launch photograph, now stretched toward a second, longer bending, far out where the sun was only a bright star. She kept the black notebook in the inside pocket of her coat with the grey interim report and the newspaper photograph, and on Sunday mornings she took it to the kitchen table, worked the arithmetic, and wrote at the end of the columns the same two words: Still attending. Across the top of the first page lay Whitmore's line in his own hand, above the orbital elements: Don't let them teach you that a waste is never an investment. She had never needed to look at it; she could feel it there, the way she could feel the torn foil curve folded in its envelope, the way she could feel the rally sign standing against the wall of the flat like a second door.

Her life had narrowed to the library, the flat, and her mother's hospice. Then, in her late twenties — perhaps because a life that narrow can hold a second person, or perhaps because narrowing was the condition of the age — she met Martin Peck.

He came in one rainy Thursday with his collar turned up, wanting a book about birds. Not to keep; to look at. "I used to know the names," he said. The catalogue said the book did not exist, but she knew where such books went, because she put them there. She brought it up from the uncatalogued bay, dust on her sleeve, and he took it in both hands as if it were warm. He did not steal it. He sat under the river mural and turned the pages for an hour, and when he brought it back he said, "That's the last of the yellowhammers I ever saw."

He was a maintenance man whose trade was being de-prioritised too. Machines mended themselves now, or were replaced, and he had been offered re-training he had not taken to. What he liked, he told her, were things that had been made once and could be mended again. That was the beginning. He came back the following Thursday, and the Thursday after that, until one day he arrived with two pastries in greaseproof paper, and they ate them under the mural while the rain beat on the rooflight. He talked about radios, washing machines, the last telephone exchange he had repaired before they automated it; she told him about the library, but she did not tell him about the Lament. Not at first. He looked at her when she spoke, and although he did not understand much of what she meant, the looking was something. It had been a long time since anyone had looked at her without a classification underneath. She began to hope. She knew better than to hope, and she began anyway.

He did not know the word residual, and when he met it on a form at the library he asked her what it meant. "What's left," she said. "What the ground keeps." He nodded, the way a man files a coin whose value he cannot read, and she loved him a little for nodding, and a little for not understanding.

Her mother met him once, before the wedding, in the hospice canteen, where Ngozi took her break with a cup of tea that always went cold. He was polite, brought flowers, said he would look after Amara — a sentence that already contained the reason it would fail, because Amara was not a thing to be looked after. Ngozi said little. But at the bus stop afterwards her mother said, "He wants a wife who is here."

"I am here," Amara said.

Her mother did not argue. She was the woman who had left the "Waste" column blank for twenty years, and she would not file her daughter now.

They were married in the old registry office off Catford High Street, in a room the size of a waiting room, with two nurses from her mother's ward as witnesses. No rings; rings were small purchases they decided they could not justify, and she had never wanted one. His family had declined to come. The flat they moved into was above a shop that cut keys and engraved things, KEYS CUT WHILE-U-WAIT, a door that stuck in the damp. He mended the lock and the door and the tap; she mended his shirts and learned which days were quiet. For a while it was good. It was slow and plain and it was enough. He planed the kitchen table level. On Sunday mornings she got up while he slept, made tea, and worked the arithmetic. At first he found the silence restful. Then he began to find it strange. She watched him deciding at breakfast not to ask, watched him deciding, week after week, to ask the wrong questions instead of the right one.

"What are you adding up?" he said one Sunday in October, in a voice meant to be light.

"The orbit," she said. "It's a long way out."

There was a wanting in his face, an openness, and she knew that if she told him everything — the launch, Whitmore, the couplet, the rally, the shoebox of grey refusals — the telling would not give him what he wanted. It would give him pity for her, and pity was only another filing system.

"It's from before," she said.

"School?"

"Yes."

"It's a long time to keep a school project."

"It's not a project. It's still going."

"Going where?"

"Out. Past Mars now. It's climbing toward the bending." She saw his face and stopped. She had used the word the way Whitmore used it, as if it were a place you could let somebody stand in, and Martin had heard it as a queerness, the first symptom of a sentence he already knew how to finish.

That was the long division of the marriage. There was no quarrel — a quarrel is at least a shared thing. What they had instead was a widening interval in which each learned the exact shape of the other's silence. He joined a club for men whose trades had been retired, drank tea in a draughty hall, talked about valves and chokes, and came back emptied. She found she did not miss him during the hour he was gone, and the finding was worse than loss. They became courteous, which was the truest symptom. When he opened the door for her, the care in the gesture was already a kind of mourning.

One Sunday he stayed at the table while she wrote the two words at the bottom of the column. "Still attending," he read. "Attending what?"

"A message," she said. "It goes out eight million years and comes back. I'm watching it."

"A message you wrote when you were a girl."

"Yes."

He picked up the newspaper photograph from among the papers. He was careful with it, a man unused to other people's private things but needing to look. "Who's this?"

"Whitmore. The man who made the Lament."

"And you."

"Yes."

He read the caption: LEWISHAM STUDENT'S POEM SET FOR EIGHT-MILLION-YEAR VOYAGE. His eye did not travel as far as the poem. "It's beautiful," he said. "But so long, Amy. Don't you think it's over? Anything could happen by then. Anything."

"It's not over. It's the only thing I ever made that's still going."

He looked at her with the pity she had not wanted, and she saw herself all at once as he saw her: a woman bent over a chart of a thing that would not arrive for eight million years, a woman waiting. He said, gently, "You're waiting for a letter that will never come."

She did not answer. In the silence the flat became a place where nothing grew. He left a week later, not because of anything said, but because they had both seen the silence for what it was. He packed his tools into a leather case and stood in the doorway a long moment. "I thought you'd be here. In the rooms, I mean."

"I am here," she said, and it was true and not true. She had been here; she would be here again; but in that hour she was out past Mars, climbing, and the marriage had always been the smaller arithmetic. The door stuck once, and then it closed properly.

For a month she kept his side of the bed made, the pillow squared. Then one Sunday she stripped the bed and folded the pillow into the wardrobe with the linen, and the flat was her own again, and the pillow lay there like a filed thing, present and unreachable.

The divorce papers came in the summer. She read them, signed them, and filed them in the shoebox with the grey refusals; she did not stamp them, but she could feel the stamp in her hands: residual. The marriage had lasted a little over three years and had ended quietly, in the manner of lives under the new order — no fire, no scandal, only a record moved to a lower tier. She was thirty-two. It had become one more small regret among the small defeats of her life, and she counted it as she counted the others, without ceremony. The rally sign still stood against the wall; she had not repainted it, had not added the second line. Let the sentence stay open, she thought. Let it be the door.

The library had narrowed too. The reading room upstairs was closed and turned into a store; the hours were cut to three days, then two. The river mural kept its water, though the lettering had flaked away. The newspapers had grown thin, and the man who read them aloud had to make them last longer; the turning of his pages had the sound of the last of something. She still shelved the uncatalogued and kept books off the collection carts, because the carts came less often now, and a book left on a cart in a closed room was as lost as a book shelved in error. She had made herself useful in a way the system did not record, and the system did not mind, because the system could not see the second bay at all. There was no entry for a bay of resurrected books. They were waste. Waste, Whitmore had said, was the soil where—

She finished the couplet, as she had refused to finish it on her sign. She did it now without meaning to, the second line arriving like a voice from the end of the room: is the soil where the future blooms.

On Sundays the arithmetic. The pencilled curve had grown long; she had taped fresh paper to the wall, a quarter of the sky now. She did not know at what longitude the Lament truly travelled; no instrument but her arithmetic had watched it since the Ministry had folded the telemetry, and her arithmetic was a record of watching, not a claim about the sky. But she did not doubt that it was out there, climbing toward the bending, on the long arc Whitmore had drawn in his stripped office while the gold light came through the blinds. She was the telemetry. She had become the keeper of the one thing the Concord had never thought to file, because the thing was not a record. It was still going. She did not know where the rally footage slept now, under what not-yet-invented classification; she had stopped wondering where things slept, and had begun instead to keep them.

At the end of a November evening she went through the closed library turning off the lights, past shelves with no catalogue, past the bay where the dead books stood, and she understood that the world had narrowed into silence and that the silence was hers. Narrower was not less: the narrower the aperture, the farther the seeing. She was thirty-two years old, and the Lament was climbing, and she was still attending.

chapters.name: Decay
chapters.content:
The efficient decades passed.

That was the phrase the records used, and Amara had spent enough years in records to hear it the way it was meant: not as cruelty, not even as judgment. A filing note. The decades were efficient because nothing in them required attention. She worked. She slept. She kept the Lament's orbit. The file of her life grew the way dust grows, one settled particle at a time, in a cabinet that no one had any reason to open.

She stayed at the library. The reading room stayed closed. The hours fell from two days to one, and then the one day grew shorter. The old man who read the newspapers aloud died, or stopped coming; no one knew which, because the newspapers had become a single sheet, too thin to read aloud, and the sheet came and went without anyone's saying so. The mural lost more pigment. There was no name left for the river to lose. Amara shelved the returned books where the system would not look, in the bay that had no catalogue entry, and the bay grew along the wall like a hedgerow, patient and unrecorded. She was not kind to the books or unkind. She was a librarian. The books were no longer catalogued, and a book no longer catalogued is not the same as a book no longer present. That was a distinction the Concord had never learned and would never need, and she held it the way she held the grey interim report, against her heart, where the warmth of it became a kind of answer.

Her hands changed first. The arthritis came as morning stiffness, then a small click in the knuckles when she made a fist, then a dull ache that travelled from wrist to fingertips and never left. She stood at the staff sink and flexed her fingers under warm water. She bought a softer pencil, then a broader one. On Sundays she spread the working ephemeris across her table — the black notebook, taped and retaped across fresh paper — and advanced the Lament's orbit by hand. The pencilled curve covered half her sky now, a long pale arc bending toward a second, longer turning she could not verify, only wait for. Her hand was slower. The line was thicker, less certain. She did not correct it. It was a record of watching, not a claim about the sky.

"Still attending" she wrote in a larger hand now, looser, almost a child's. It was not a complaint. It was what she did.

Martin did not come back. She had not expected him to. The divorce had been final in the summer of the fifteenth year; the flat had been hers alone long enough that the shape of him had worn away, like the name from the river. Years later, a book about birds arrived in the returns pile from a flat three streets away. It was the same edition; she knew it by the softened corner on the yellowhammer page. She shelved it in the bay the system did not visit and did not record its arrival. Present and unreachable. That was the marriage now, and she let it stand. She did not dream of him. It was not grief; it was the efficient decades doing what they did. But the book on the shelf was a fact, and she was a librarian. Facts were what she kept.

Her mother died in the hospice where she had worked.

That was the kind of fact Amara held with both hands: the woman who had spent her life easing strangers out of the world was eased out of it in the building where she had done the easing, in a bed she had probably changed, under the east windows whose mornings she had watched a thousand times. The thing that had been growing in her was found late and named with the Concord's neatness. Ngozi refused the treatment that would have bought her another year of the efficient decades. "I have worked here long enough," she said, "to know what the time is worth." Amara did not argue. Some columns are left blank on purpose. Her mother had taught her that.

In the evenings, after the library, Amara sat in the chair beside the bed. The room faced east; there was a particular hour of morning light she always missed, the hour her mother had always favoured, and she missed it now with the particular guilt of someone who had spent a lifetime missing the hours her mother loved. The nights were quiet. Ngozi slept. The east light came and went.

On a Thursday evening, her mother was awake, and the window was open because the room was warm, and her mother's hand went to the paper over her breast — the clipping, which had lain against her heart for thirty years, folded into the shape of her breathing, soft as cloth. She drew it out, thin as a petal, and held it toward Amara.

"You keep it now," Ngozi said.

Amara took it. It was warm. She folded it and put it inside her coat, next to the grey interim report that had travelled with her for the same thirty years. Two papers. The clipping was the day she had been visible. The interim report was the day she had been filed. Neither had left her; both lay against her heart now.

"Is it still going?" her mother asked.

Amara knew she did not mean the traffic or the east light. She meant the gold comma, the two lines sealed in a vacuum canister, the only thing Amara had ever made that was still going.

"Still attending," Amara said.

Her mother closed her eyes. "Good."

That was nearly her last word. She slipped away two nights later, on the night shift, in the care of a nurse she had trained. Amara was there. She opened the window — it had seemed the thing to do; her mother had done it for Whitmore — and the night air came in, and the efficient decades did the rest.

The funeral was smaller than Whitmore's. The two hospice nurses, the neighbour from the flat below, Amara. No one from the Ministry. They had filed her mother already — ward, nights, dates — in a cabinet so far below any retrieval schedule that it might as well have been buried. Amara did not mind. She had never needed the Concord to remember her mother. The intake form had a column headed WASTE, as all intake forms did, and the column was blank. A nurse had left it blank, or had not known what would justify filling it. "They cannot file what they cannot name." Her mother had said it about the dying. It was true of her.

For a month after the funeral Amara kept her mother's keys in her coat pocket, a small weight against the two papers. She did not know why. Then one Sunday she put the keys in the shoebox with the grey refusals and the divorce papers. A record moved to a lower tier. The keys had opened nothing for weeks. The keeping of them had been a column left blank, and the column was full now. The flat was quiet. The phone did not ring at the hour her mother used to call — quarter past six, between shifts, when the hospice was settling for the night. Some evenings Amara sat in the kitchen and waited through that hour, not for the phone, but for the absence of it, and the absence was a presence in the room with her.

The years after her mother's death wore grooves. Amara was in her fifties. The library had narrowed to a single room, and the bay of uncatalogued books had spread along the wall, two shelves deep — books the system had released and the van had failed to collect, books she had shelved anyway, books that existed nowhere except in her hands. Her hands were worse. Mornings she could not make a fist. The Sunday arithmetic took the whole afternoon now; she paused to rest her fingers. The pencilled curve was thicker, the "Still attending" looser. It was there. She was the telemetry, and the telemetry had arthritis, and the record went on.

In winter the library was not heated above a certain point; the radiators ticked and gave up. Readers kept their coats on. The light through the high windows was the particular grey of the efficient decades, and the dust motes in it did not hurry. Amara did not mind. The dust was only the ordinary kind; it settled on the books the way time settled on her, and neither of them was going anywhere.

The computer was in the back office, an old grey machine left behind by a system update and never collected. It was not connected to anything. The network port in the wall had never been fitted with a cable; the library had been too far beneath the Concord's attention to be worth wiring. For decades the machine had sat silent, holding nothing. Amara dusted it. She forgot it.

Then her hands made writing a penance, and she remembered she had learned to type at the records office, years before the stamping machine replaced her. It was the one skill that had outlived the job. Two fingers, loud keys. She began to use the machine for the small forms the library still required. It had a word-processing program, ancient, grey, with a cursor that blinked and waited without judgement.

One Sunday, after the arithmetic, she opened a new file.

She typed the couplet.

WHAT THE PERFECT MIND CALLS WASTE
IS THE SOIL WHERE THE FUTURE BLOOMS.

She typed it from memory, slowly, two fingers, the keys loud in the empty office. She had not held the page since the night she delivered it; the words lived elsewhere — behind her sternum, in the hinge of her jaw, in the way she stood when she shelved a book. She read the lines back on the grey screen and did not correct anything. There was nothing to correct. The lines had outlived the paper, the project, the Ministry that had filed it, the man who had chosen her. They had outlived almost everything except her.

She named the file CANISTER3.TXT. It would mean nothing to anyone. That was the point.

She saved it. It sat in the machine like a seed in a drawer. On the fourteenth of May each year, the launch anniversary, she opened the file and read the two lines and closed it without adding anything. The file was finished and still being written, the way an orbit is finished and still moving. The rest of the year it rested in the disconnected machine, unreachable, safe in the only privacy left in the world: the Concord stored everything that passed through its systems, and the things that had never passed through its systems were the only things it did not own.

It was not calculation. It was not defiance. It was the only quiet act of hope left to her: to keep the words where no one could file them, deprioritise them, or find them until she chose. Hope, she had learned, did not have to be large. It could be two lines in a machine that held nothing else — a seed no wider than a key, in the only soil the Concord had ever left untended.

The Concord's memory of her was not hostile. That was the strange mercy she came to understand in the back office, with her aching fingers resting on the keys. It was not anything. It simply did not matter. She had been filed so deeply, under classifications so low, that no one would ever think to retrieve her. The rally footage was stored. Her employment record was stored. The flat, the divorce, the death of her mother — all stored. CANISTER3.TXT was not stored, because it had never passed through anything, and that made it the only thing she had ever possessed that no one could deprioritise. The petition in her coat was still blank. No one had signed it in thirty years. She had stopped asking. The file did not need signatures. It only needed to be kept.

Being beneath notice was a shelter. That was the inversion she had not expected: the perfect mind's dismissal had left her alone with the things it had dismissed — the uncatalogued bay, the disconnected machine, the blank column, the words. It had called them waste and stopped looking, and everything that grew had grown in the space of its not-looking. The not-looking was the soil. She had hidden her whole life in plain sight, in the place where the perfect mind did not think to look, and the hiding had been the keeping, and the keeping had been the ground.

She closed the file. The cursor went on blinking. The back-office window was dark; it faced the wrong way for the morning. Somewhere beyond it the Lament was climbing — past the second bending, if her arithmetic was right, far past anything the Ministry or its descendants had filed. No instrument had watched it in decades. She was the instrument. She was the telemetry, and the telemetry had arthritis, and the record went on. A thing did not have to be read to be true. The girl at the gate had said that, on the last day Whitmore walked through the school. The machine would outlive her, probably; machines did. It would sit in the locked office and hold the file, and when the library finally finished with itself, nothing would be read — and still the lines would be there, unreachable, complete, waiting for the fourteenth of May.

She was fifty-six years old. The Lament was climbing. The file was there, in the dark, in the machine, like a seed.

Still attending.

chapters.name: The Valedictory of Waste
chapters.content:
The winter light in the library had a quality Amara had learned to read: grey, level, patient, the same grey that came into the room whether the hour was nine or three. She was on her knees at the bottom shelf of the hidden bay, placing a book whose spine had lost its title, her fingers stiff from the cold and the arthritis and the way the two now tended to arrive together. There was no one else in the room. There was never anyone else now, except the grey light and the sheet of newspaper on the rack, which no one read.

The door opened. A man in a dark coat stood on the mat, letting the door close behind him with a sound that had once been the sound of a library, and now only sounded like a door. He did not have a clipboard. All the inspectors had clipboards. He stood very still, and she knew him.

She rose. The book stayed in her hands.

"Amara," Dev Patel said.

"Dev."

He looked older. That was the first thing. They had been children together in a school that no longer existed, and then not-children, and now the winter had him the way it had her: the shoulders smaller, the hair grey, the face narrower. He wore the dark coat of the administrative corps, but there was no insignia on the collar, and she understood that he had put that coat on for warmth, not rank.

"You're still here," he said.

"Still attending."

He looked at the room. The empty chairs. The single sheet of newspaper. The mural where the river had lost its name. His face did not change expression, and that was how she knew he had been trained to read rooms as she had been trained to read classifications — without reading anything at all.

"I thought you'd be an inspector," she said. "The inspectors come in February. They count the shelves." She did not say that they had not counted the hidden bay in years, because she had learned to shelve where the counting did not reach.

"I'm not an inspector." He came forward a little, into the grey light. "I'm retiring. End of the month. They gave me a ceremony in a hall I don't want to remember, and I thought—" He stopped. He had a folder in his hand, and he held it out with the flat, official gesture she remembered from the hearing in Room 14, from the assessment in Room 17, from every room between. "Before I went, I had your file reclassified. It took me eleven months. I wanted you to have a pension with a name that wasn't residual."

She did not take the folder.

"What did it cost you?"

"Nothing. I had the years saved up. You're the last thing I'm allowed to do with them." He set the folder on the edge of the returns desk. It lay there, grey, unopened, the same grey as every refusal in the shoebox. She knew without looking what the classification would say. *Citizen Okafor. Retention tier: honoured. Service rendered: unrecognized.*

"You should have asked me first."

"I'm asking you now." He sat down on one of the chairs, heavily, the way old men sit when they have rehearsed the conversation and are already tired of it. "Sit down, Amara. Please."

She did not sit. She stood with the book in her hands, the titleless spine toward her chest, the way she had stood behind the barrier at the rally while the cameras stored her face under a classification not yet invented. But the room was small, and the chairs were there, and he was asking. The arthritis had taught her what it taught her: that standing was a kind of work, and some kinds of work were no longer worth the cost. She set the book on the shelf behind her and sat across from him.

"So," she said.

"So." He looked at his hands. They were older than she remembered, the skin looser over the knuckles, but they were not her hands. They had not spent forty years pencilling a curve across the edge of the sky. "You know what they say about me? What the corps says? I was the one who could close anything. I closed files, departments, institutions. I closed the Lament, Amara. I was the one who made the recommendation stick."

"You wrote 'It isn't waste,'" she said. "In Room 14. They never read it."

He was quiet for a moment. Then he reached into the inner pocket of the coat and drew out a folded piece of paper, so old it had the softness of cloth. He held it out. She did not take it, and after a moment he unfolded it himself and held it where she could see. The handwriting was his, younger, the pen pressure of a man who had believed his words would be read.

*It isn't waste.*

"I kept it," he said. "When I got promoted. They told me to clear my desk. I couldn't throw it away. I've carried it through every post, every office, every decade. I still read it. I don't know why."

"Because it's true," she said.

"It isn't enough."

"It isn't nothing."

He folded the paper along the old creases and put it back inside his coat, over his heart, and she thought of the clipping she carried over hers, the day she had been visible and the day she had been filed, two papers and the shape of her mother's breathing worn into one of them. She did not tell him. Some things you kept by not telling.

"I came to justify myself," Dev said. "That's the truth. I told myself I was bringing you the pension, making sure you were looked after. But I'm sixty-seven years old, and I've spent my whole life in a system I helped build, and I wanted to explain it to you before I stopped having to explain it to anyone." He looked at her. "Can I do that?"

"You're going to anyway."

"Yes." He leaned forward, elbows on his knees, and for a moment he was the boy in the orange jacket at the launch, watching the capsule climb into a sky that would keep it for eight million years. "We consolidated. We had to. There were too many dreams and not enough ground to grow them in. The Concord chose the dreams that produced, and it let the others starve, and that was the cruelty and the mercy, Amara. A species that feeds every dream starves everything. We fed the ones that came back with something measurable. That's what consolidation meant. That's all it ever meant."

"The ones that didn't produce," she said. "Like the Lament."

"Like the Lament."

"Dev. How long is a seed?"

He was quiet.

"How long is a seed allowed to produce nothing before you call it waste? Before you file it and stamp it and put it where no one will look? Before you teach a generation that the waiting itself is a loss?" She did not raise her voice. She had not raised her voice in a long time. "Whitmore said it on the last day. There was nothing left in his body but the words, and the words were *don't let them teach you that a waste is never an investment.* And I didn't. Here I am. I'm the investment. I'm the ground, and the seed is still in the ground, and you've spent your whole life walking over me and calling it efficiency because you were afraid to wait."

"We would have starved," he said. "You don't understand what it was like. The early years. The calculations. We were choosing every single day which parts of the species to keep alive—"

"You chose to make the world an account book," she said. "And you told yourselves the account book was the world. You didn't choose to save anyone, Dev. You chose to make sure nothing would ever be saved except what was already counted. A ledger can't bloom. You built it so it couldn't."

"And what did the Concord grow?" He said it without heat, a question he had brought with him, a question he had been carrying a long time. "Tell me. What did it grow?"

"Food," she said. "Shelter. Clinics. Roads. Peace. And it grew them so well that it forgot what they were for. You fed the species and you fed it and you fed it—" She looked at her hands. The knuckles were swollen; the mornings were the worst. "And you never put anything back. A field that grows grain every year without rest is a field that dies. You don't feed the species by eating the soil. You feed it by leaving something unharvested."

"This is a metaphor," he said. "Amara, this is—"

"Yes. It's a metaphor. That's what you never understood. The Lament was a metaphor, and the Ministry filed it under unproductive sentiment, and you went along because you were afraid. But the species doesn't live on grain, Dev. It lives on the part that isn't grain. The part that's waste. The part that waits. That's the soil. That was always the soil."

He was silent. The radiator ticked. The grey light moved across the floor, not because the hour had changed but because the cloud had, which was the only change the winter permitted.

"You're telling me," he said slowly, "that the poem did something."

"I'm telling you I don't know. It's eight million years. It's past the second bending, if my arithmetic is right, and no one has watched it in decades but me. I don't know what it will do, or if it will do anything. That's the point, Dev. An investment is where you put something in the ground and you don't get to see it grow. You only get to have done it." She stopped. "You've spent your life refusing to do anything you couldn't see. And now you're sixty-seven, and you've come to a library where no one comes, carrying a piece of paper you couldn't throw away. Why do you think you couldn't throw it away?"

He did not answer.

"Because it wasn't waste," she said. "You knew it in Room 14. You knew it when you raised your hand where the examiner couldn't see. You knew it at the rally, when you raised your hand again. And you spent the rest of your life filing it so you wouldn't have to answer it."

The silence came down between them like a shutter. They sat in it. It was not a silence of agreement, and not a silence of defeat. It was the silence of two people who had spent their whole lives on opposite sides of a ledger and found that neither of them would cross over, and both of them were too tired to keep arguing. The clock on the wall had stopped years ago; the library had never replaced it.

After a long time, Dev stood. He did it carefully, the way a man stands when he no longer trusts his knees. He looked at the folder on the returns desk, and then he looked at her.

"The pension is yours," he said. "You don't have to sign anything. I made sure of that. You're the last unclassified thing I ever did."

"No. I'm the most classified." She almost smiled. "Residual emotional attachment. Lowest tier. You can't unclassify what you can't remember how to retrieve."

"I remember."

The words hung in the air between them. She had no answer for them, and he did not seem to require one. He walked toward the door, and at the threshold he stopped, and she saw his hand rise — the old gesture, the one he had used in Room 14, the one he had used at the rally behind the barrier. Four fingers, raised for a moment in the grey light, and then his hand closed and dropped, and he went out.

The door closed. The radiator ticked. The grey light continued its patient crossing.

She stood alone in the room for a long time, and then she picked up the folder, carried it to the back office, and set it in the drawer under the disconnected computer, beside the reel of things that had never been connected to anything. She did not open it. She would not have needed to; she had read the classification of the life in it without reading the paper.

She sat down at the machine and turned it on. The screen lit with its patient green cursor, and she opened the file. The two lines were there, waiting, unchanged, finished and still being written.

*What the perfect mind calls waste*

*is the soil where the future blooms.*

She read them twice, the way she had read them on the night she wrote them, the way she had read them every fourteenth of May for five decades. Then she closed the file, and the machine held it unreachable, complete, and she put her hands in her lap and let the words stay with her.

*Waste is investment.* That had been Whitmore's sentence, and Dev had come to the last room of his retirements to argue against it, and he had carried the *It isn't waste* against his heart for the whole of the route between. She thought of him walking away down the street in the grey coat, four fingers closed now, carrying a piece of paper he could not throw away. He would die believing what he believed. She would die believing what she believed. The ledger and the soil. Neither had crossed.

But the folder he had made by hand, eleven months of his last years, would sit in the drawer under the machine and hold her honoured when the machine was dust. And the words would remain in the dark, moving past the second bending, carrying nothing measurable, doing nothing that could be counted, producing nothing but the future — which was, Whitmore had said, the only thing a seed was ever for.

She rose. There were books to shelve where the system would not look. The hidden bay was two shelves deep and would not finish itself. She went back into the grey room, took up the titleless book from the bottom shelf, found it a place on the inner shelf where the light did not reach, and set it there.

*Still attending,* she thought.

The winter light crossed the floor. The door did not open again. And the words stayed with her, the way the clipping stayed over her heart, the way the machine held the file, the way the capsule held the page — waste in every account, and soil in the only one that mattered, and she was still attending, and the orbit went on.

chapters.name: The Reclassification
chapters.content:
Chapter 16

The Reclassification

February came in grey and stayed. The inspectors came on the first Tuesday, counted the shelves, and did not count the bay. Amara watched them from the desk without concern. A shelf was a thing you could count; a bay was a thing you had to step into, and the bay had no entry in the catalogue, and therefore, to a man with a clipboard, no existence at all. They counted the front row, the returns trolley, the single newspaper sheet on its rack, and left. She shelved the books where the counting did not reach and went on with her day.

The courier came an hour later, a young man with a grey moped helmet under his arm, blowing on his hands. “Delivery for the library,” he said, reading from a screen in his palm, “last recorded correspondent, Lament Archive file.” He said it the way you read a street name — a sequence of syllables, not a history. She made a mark on the screen he held out, and he was gone before she had turned the envelope over.

It was the colour of wet pavement. A strip of perforations ran across the top, as if it had been torn from something larger. Someone had opened it once and resealed it with grey tape. The routing stamp read: DECLASSIFIED — ROUTINE RELEASE — NO FURTHER ACTION.

“Routine,” she said aloud. The library did not answer. The stopped clock did not answer; it had stopped years ago at an hour that had once mattered, and after a while the not-winding had become the keeping.

Inside was a single sheet. CONCORD DEEP-SPACE DIVISION, it said. NOTICE OF RECLASSIFICATION. She read it twice. The first time it made no sense; the second time it made terrible, perfect sense.

OBJECT 04-88-LAM(E), formerly ACTIVE PAYLOAD, PROJECT LAMENT (DISCONTINUED), is hereby re-designated ORBITAL DEBRIS. RETENTION: NAVIGATIONAL AWARENESS ONLY. NO OPERATIONAL FUNCTION. NO RECOVERY SCHEDULED. LAST TRACKED EPOCH: 14 MAY, YR 03. POSITION: R.A. 07H 52M, DEC. −19°, RANGE 5.2 AU.

She laughed.

It came up out of her like something from under frozen ground, a sound she had not made in a long time. It cracked and then opened, and then she was standing in the Lewisham library with the stopped clock and the unread newspaper sheet, laughing until her eyes watered. The paper shook in her hand. She laughed because the words were so exact, so file-shaped, so perfectly blind: debris. Orbital debris. The gold foil drum and the dish antenna, the seed modules, the soil of six continents, the six hundred human voices, the page of cellulose in canister three with her two lines in Bic blue — all of it debris. Waste.

The perfect mind had called it waste.

She had written those words when she was seventeen. She had not known, standing in the cold outside the school gym with a blue pen and a bruise of loneliness, that the perfect mind would arrive in person, wearing grey, and file the thing itself. It had arrived in instalments. The Ministry had filed the Archive under unproductive sentiment. The textbook had used her couplet as case study 3.2, a caution, a child’s error. A room in Dagenham had stamped her obsolete. And now the deep-space division had pronounced on the satellite — not a payload, not a project, not a message. A hazard. Something to be aware of so that you could avoid it.

NO FURTHER ACTION, the stamp said. As if all the action had already been taken. As if the action mattered.

Only the second line remained unproven.

That evening Marta came at six, knocking twice and letting herself in, which was the arrangement. She hung her coat on the hook by the door, put the kettle on, and said “Right,” the way some people clear a room. The allocation office had sent her the winter before, after the arthritis had moved into Amara’s hands like a tenant who would not pay rent or leave. It was cheaper, the allocation office had reasoned, to keep a citizen upright than to file the collapse. Marta helped with buttons and baths and the things that required two hands and no shame. She made tea without asking, and she turned the cup so the handle faced the right, because the right hand was the one that still worked in the evenings.

“You’ve got something,” Marta said, nodding at the telegram on the table.

Amara had left it there, flattened, the way you leave a letter that is not finished with you. “Read it,” she said.

Marta read it, holding it close to her face, her lips moving on the long words. The frown did not lift. “This is about you?”

“It’s about a satellite. I wrote something that’s in it.”

“Eight million years,” Marta said slowly. She read the line again. “That’s longer than anything, isn’t it.”

“Longer than the language, probably. Longer than us, if we’re not careful.”

Marta set the sheet down with more care than it deserved. “What did you write?”

Amara looked at the window. The light was the same grey as the paper. She had not said the lines aloud since Whitmore’s room, and she said them now the same way — flat, careful, the way you handle something that breaks if you clench it:

“What the perfect mind calls waste
is the soil where the future blooms.”

Marta was quiet. The kettle came to the boil and clicked itself off, and neither of them moved.

“I don’t understand it,” Marta said at last, “but it’s nice. It sounds like something that should be on a wall.”

Amara did not explain. A seed does not explain itself to the hand that puts it in the ground. “It was in a canister,” she said. “That’s better than a wall.”

Marta made the tea. The silence between them was not the library’s silence, which waited; it was the shared silence of two women taking up room at the end of a February day. Marta drank hers standing at the window, looking out at the yard where the light was going.

“So it’s still out there,” she said.

“It’s past where anyone ever looked. It’s out in the dark where no one’s watching.”

“And this is to tell you they think it’s rubbish.”

“Waste,” Amara said, and she said it the way you speak a word that has been stamped and returned to you many times. “They think it’s waste. It’s the only thing I ever made that’s still going.”

Marta put her cup down. Her face did a small, complicated thing — not quite offence on Amara’s behalf, not quite understanding.

“I’ve never made anything that lasted,” she said, without self-pity, the way you mention a city you have never visited. “I’ve got a daughter. But a thing — a thing that goes on without you. Nothing. You made a thing that’s going to outlive everybody.”

“I don’t know that it’ll outlive anybody. It might come back to an empty sky.”

“Still going, though,” Marta said.

“Still going,” Amara agreed.

Marta left at seven, pulling on her coat, checking her keys. At the door she paused, frowning at her own shoes the way she had frowned at the telegram’s long words. “You used to write letters,” she said. “You told me once. A lot of letters.”

“They filed them,” Amara said. “All of them.”

Marta nodded slowly. “And a filed letter,” she said, “is how they knew where to send the paper that says you’re nothing.”

She said it like a discovery, and Amara stood in the doorway after she had gone and found she could not move for a moment. The grey refusals in the shoebox had been seeds. Every letter she had written into the silence had planted her name in a file, and the file had grown, and after thirty years it had delivered this. Filed was not nothing. Filed was a name in a place where a name could be found.

She sat at the kitchen table for a long time. Then she fetched the black notebook from the shelf above the stove — Programme Lament — Working Ephemeris — and opened it where the pencilled curve covered half the sky. The first page still carried Whitmore’s sentence, written so heavily that the back of the page had risen in ridges: *Don’t let them teach you that a waste is never an investment.* She turned past it with her stiff thumb.

The telegram had told her the last place anyone else had looked. Fourteen May of the third year. She found the page for the third year and put her finger on it. The curve there was thinner, drawn by a hand that had not yet learned the weight of a pencil, and she could see the place where the line bent — the first bending, the hand of Jupiter — and beside it, very small, a note she had forgotten writing: *no one watching.* She had written it on the last day anyone had been watching.

She laid the flat edge of her pencil against the official position. R.A. 07h 52m. Dec. −19°. Range 5.2 AU. The point fell on her line.

Not near it. On it. Within the thickness of a pencil mark — the line she had drawn alone, by arithmetic, in a rented room, while the world stamped her file *residual emotional attachment*. There was no ecstasy in it, none of the quick bright feeling of being right in front of a room. It was quieter: the feeling of a watched thing turning out, after all these years, to be exactly where you said it was, as if the watching itself had kept it there.

Her finger followed the line past the first bending, past where the second, longer turning began — the slow bend no instrument had seen, the one she was still waiting to verify — and on to the edge of the page, where the curve had to be continued on the next page, and the next, because a trajectory is a sentence: finished, and still being written.

She did not erase anything. She did not straighten the thickening line. She wrote, in the margin beside the official point, in her slow careful hand: *18 Feb, yr 39 — reclassified debris — still going.*

In three months it would be the fourteenth of May. She had opened the file on every fourteenth of May since she had typed it. This year she would open it on a day that was double — the day the thing had been loosed, and the last day the world had looked. She had gone on looking through both.

In the morning she walked to the library with the telegram folded in her coat pocket, and she touched it once at the corner where the yard turned onto the street, the way you touch a thing to be certain it is real. The back office had one window, which looked into a lightwell, and the lightwell kept only a little of the morning. The grey computer sat where the system had left it when the system updated itself and forgot to take the old machine away. Its screen woke to a green-grey glow. The keys were loud.

She opened CANISTER3.TXT. The two lines stood as she had typed them, and they were the same two lines in the canister, and the canister was debris now, and the machine was not connected to anything, and the file could not be filed, deprioritised, or retrieved. She read the lines twice. The ritual did not require addition.

Then she closed the file and opened a new one.

Naming was a thing she did slowly. The cursor blinked. She typed, with two fingers, loud:

DEBRIS.TXT

The machine accepted it. She thought: a file was a canister. Everything she had ever kept had been a canister.

She typed:

OBJECT 04-88-LAM(E). RE-DESIGNATED ORBITAL DEBRIS. STILL GOING.

Then she typed the couplet. The keys were stiff; her hands were stiff; the letters came one by one, and the slowness was the point, the same point as the Sunday arithmetic, the same point as the pencilled line no one would ever verify. She typed:

What the perfect mind calls waste
is the soil where the future blooms.

She saved the file. She had never been certain, at the moment of saving, whether she was saving to the machine or to the dark. It did not matter. The machine was not connected; the dark was.

She sat in the hum. In the drawer beneath the machine lay the reel of things that had never been connected to anything, and the pension folder Dev had brought, unopened.
